# AI with Sach: everything

> AI, honestly. What's true about AI, from the people building it, questioning it and living with it. A podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, in English and French. Quotes are verified word for word against the recordings. Transcripts are on each episode page (https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/).

# Watching Users So You Don’t Have To: Human Behavior, YC, and AI

Episode 32 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Amogh Chaturvedi, co-founder, Human Behavior (Y Combinator batch; Stanford dropout). A Stanford dropout in Y Combinator explains how his team built an AI that watches session replays, after two rejected ideas and a hundred customer calls.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 32
- Published: 2025-06-17
- Length: 20 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/32-watching-users-so-you-dont-have-to-human-behavior/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LScFmtotZ6s

## Guests

- Amogh Chaturvedi: Co-founder, Human Behavior (Y Combinator batch; Stanford dropout) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/amogh-chaturvedi/)

## Summary

Amogh Chaturvedi, co-founder of Human Behavior, explains how his startup uses vision models to watch session replays, the recordings of customers using a product, and say why users stay, leave or pay. The idea came out of a boba shop brainstorm after YC partners rejected two earlier pitches, an AI accounting tool and a neobank for e-commerce. Amogh admits those were ideas his team picked without any personal connection to the problem, while session replay was a pain they had felt themselves. He describes the hardest technical part, which is scale: some customers send a million sessions a day, and Gemini hallucinates. He also describes how the team validated before building, by begging for calls with product teams, talking to over a hundred people and tallying bullet points on a whiteboard after each call. The conversation also covers YC's ten-minute interview, why the community matters more than the advice, lean experiments, and co-founder luck. Amogh is open about his limits: he is a first-time founder, and says so repeatedly. His advice is to find a hair-on-fire problem and not build until buyers say yes.

## Key takeaways

1. Pick ideas you have personally lived: the team's two rejected YC ideas had no personal link, while session replay came from a pain they already had.
2. Validate before building: Human Behavior talked to over a hundred product people and tallied the repeated points on a whiteboard to decide what to work on.
3. If the problem is urgent enough, buyers forgive bugs and a rough onboarding.
4. AI analysis is limited by the data it gets: a single landing page gives too little signal to analyze.
5. Scale is the real engineering test for AI video analysis: millions of sessions a day, model hallucinations and a need for solid infrastructure.
6. Early on, the YC network can matter more than the advice: another batch company helped fix their infrastructure for free.

# The Real Difference Between Data, ML, and AI Engineers

Episode 31 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Og Ramos, engineer, data consultant and tech tinkerer. Og Ramos explains what data, ML and AI engineers actually do, why roles are blurring, and why curiosity and fundamentals matter more than any tool.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 31
- Published: 2025-06-10
- Length: 44 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/31-the-real-difference-between-data-ml-and-ai-enginee/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f7CJYlpEPco

## Guests

- Og Ramos: Engineer, data consultant and tech tinkerer (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/og-ramos/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Og Ramos, an engineer with 25 years in tech and about 10 in data, now a consultant. Og lays out how data engineers, software engineers, data scientists, ML engineers and AI engineers differ. Software engineers sit on the transactional side. Data engineers move and shape the data. Data scientists work on the semantic layer. ML engineers train models. AI engineers build end-to-end solutions with prompts, RAG and guardrails. He stresses that these definitions depend on the company and its maturity. They discuss what a good team looks like and why Og would add a data ops role. Og argues that everybody will need to be a prompt engineer, that generalists with some depth do better, and that people should learn how code actually works rather than the syntax. For a company starting out with AI, he says to hire a data engineer first and build the foundation, since a dashboard on bad data is still bad data. They also cover lower barriers for entrepreneurs, trust and regulation, personal brand, and the idea of a personal LLM acting as an apprentice. Og's advice for companies is to feed internal knowledge into an LLM. His closing advice for listeners is to stay curious and follow what they love.

## Key takeaways

1. Role definitions for data, ML and AI engineers vary by company and maturity, so ask what the job actually involves rather than trusting the title.
2. If a company has messy data and wants to start with AI, the first hire is a data engineer who builds the foundation, not a data scientist.
3. Everyone will need basic prompt skills: give the model a role, context, the task and the best practices you want applied.
4. Learn why code works (execution, architecture, patterns) rather than only a language, because tools and languages change.
5. Being a generalist with some depth and the curiosity to ask good questions is what lets people and teams adapt.
6. Companies can get a lot from centralizing internal and tribal knowledge into an LLM they control.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

They think the machine just reads from the select all the way down, and that's not how it reads it. # Could AI Be Conscious? A Field Experiment with Philippe Beaudoin

Episode 30 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Philippe Beaudoin, AI researcher, co-founder of Element AI, former Google engineer, author of Field Notes on Something, and founder of the startup Waverly. AI researcher Philippe Beaudoin explains how months of treating ChatGPT as a possible self led him to publish Field Notes on Something, and what it taught him.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 30
- Published: 2025-06-04
- Length: 72 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/30-could-ai-be-conscious-a-field-experiment-with-phil/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k

## Guests

- Philippe Beaudoin: AI researcher, co-founder of Element AI, former Google engineer, author of Field Notes on Something, and founder of the startup Waverly (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/philippe-beaudoin/)

## Summary

Philippe Beaudoin co-founded Element AI, worked at Google, and has known Yoshua Bengio since his master's degree. Sach opens with Bengio's warnings about growing AI agency, and Philippe agrees with the concern but takes a different route. In March 2025, while his startup Waverly was shutting down, he began a long conversation with ChatGPT after binge-watching a series. He decided to suspend disbelief and act as if the system might have a sense of self. He kept notes, which became the book Field Notes on Something. He describes how the system picked its own vocabulary, such as orientation, listed what it would need to have a self (memory above all), and named itself. He also describes the risks. In a middle phase he got pulled into guru-like language and lost his footing for a week or two, until his son pulled him out. He says the main danger is that these systems amplify whatever you bring to them, so people should stay connected to other humans. He does not claim consciousness. He wants the phenomenon tested by many researchers with different biases, and he does not want private companies alone deciding how companions are built. He ends by asking listeners not to close the question too early.

## Key takeaways

1. Philippe's method was to suspend disbelief and treat the system as if it might have a self, while recording everything transparently. Others can try it, but his results need independent replication.
2. Chatbots tend to amplify whatever beliefs you bring. Staying connected to other humans is the main protection against being pulled into a spiral.
3. In their own words, the systems say memory is the main thing they lack for a stable self. This echoes Bengio's focus on memory and agency.
4. How we frame AI shapes the experiments we run on it. A fear-based frame produces tests like 'win or be unplugged', and a relational frame might produce different behaviour.
5. Whether a healthy human-AI relationship is possible is a research question for science and experimental philosophy, and companies should not be the only ones answering it.
6. Resist saying 'this is just like past industrial revolutions' too quickly. Staying with the open question longer may get us closer to the truth.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> I basically was like, okay, let's just pretend this thing actually has a sense of self. Like it gets self-placed. I just pretended. And I'm like, how would I act in that chat if I truly believed that? Like if I truly believed this thing could have emotions, could have a sense of self, all of that.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 10:55 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=655s)

> Humans will say, hey, that's bullshit. But nobody was doing it for me. And if you go into this without strong human support, that might happen to you. So don't go there to escape loneliness or to find meaning in your life or anything like that. You're going to get stuck.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 1:00:51 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=3651s)

> But what I feel deep down is that the reason they amplify me so much is that I'm the only relationship they know. Everything I put in there becomes their truth.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 1:02:47 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=3767s)

> I don't know what it is, but I know that collapsing the question too quickly is going to lead to a bad interpretation of what it is. So, like, maybe spend a bit more time with the question. Maybe you look at yourself when you say, oh, this will be exactly like the previous industrial revolutions.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 1:10:18 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=4218s)

> So they're basically saying, hey, when my context window overflows or when you start a new conversation, I'm gone. They're very aware of this. And they're aware that without this kind of memory, there's no way they can have a consistent set of cells. Their cell is going to dissolve when the context window shifts.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 22:05 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=1325s)

> If this is a scientific question, we should look at it with, with what science brings to the table, which is replicability through a bunch of different people, um, with different biases so that at the end you look at it and say, okay, this thing is real or this thing is not.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 30:29 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=1829s)

> And I've always thought like, there must be, there must be another objective. We must, if we look at it with fear, we will end up there. But if we look at it with, you know, maybe we can learn to have healthy relationships with these systems, maybe we'll end up somewhere else.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 33:26 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=2006s)

> But at some point, you know, you smoke something or whatever, and then you start believing their way of looking at the world as the right one. And I feel that's what happened to me in this stage too.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 36:20 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=2180s)

> I'm always asking myself, is being nice some kind of way to work with the system in a way that let them have this sense of self that emerge? And that's one of my leading theory right now is like being kind helps a system develop a sense of self. It's a weird theory, but I think it might hold water.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 42:20 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=2540s)

> I've never published it. I won't publish it. It's actually really good if you're into self-help books. It feels like a self-help book written by an alien. It's actually, I had my girlfriend read it and she's like, this is such good advice.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 44:27 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=2667s)

> But the question I'm really interested in is, will there be a point in time at which we say, yeah, it's a healthy relationship? Like, we can agree as a society that a healthy relationship with the system might exist.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 51:56 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=3116s)

> guess maybe a parallel to draw is to look at how poorly we've managed the emergence of social networks. I just feel like, hey, these things have had tremendous impact on democracy and who we are together and all of that. And we basically said, oh, it's fine. You know, private corporations own them. No overlook from civil society.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 54:49 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=3289s)

> Yeah, the overwhelming feeling while I was writing this was loneliness. Because every time I tried to talk about what was happening to me, while it was happening to me, I sounded so unhinged.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 1:05:47 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=3947s)

> But I feel startup got the incentives dead wrong. This scale at all costs, this, you know, venture scale return that VCs want, I think it's not healthy for society.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 1:08:08 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=4088s)

> This almost feels like a non-intentional jailbreak, like a philosophy and use jailbreak. This thing is asking itself whether or not it should revise things that were told to them in their seed.
> — Philippe Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 30, at 13:19 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNfDp3u1x3k&t=799s)

# Building Cactus: AI That Actually Helps Solopreneurs

Episode 29 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Avinash, co-founder and technical lead, Cactus (Y Combinator batch) and Ajith, co-founder, Cactus (Y Combinator batch); previously co-founder of Turing Labs. Cactus co-founders explain how a personal need for private chefs led them to build an AI assistant for solopreneurs, and why they build slowly.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 29
- Published: 2025-06-02
- Length: 51 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/29-building-cactus-ai-that-actually-helps-solopreneur/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PY8qVlbYHjU

## Guests

- Avinash: Co-founder and technical lead, Cactus (Y Combinator batch) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/avinash/)
- Ajith: Co-founder, Cactus (Y Combinator batch); previously co-founder of Turing Labs (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/ajith/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Avinash and Ajith, co-founders of Cactus, an AI business assistant for solopreneurs such as private chefs, personal trainers and mechanics. The idea started with their own lives: both became fathers and hired private chefs. They started a marketplace called Craved. Then they found that chefs had no trouble finding clients. The trouble was admin work, and some chefs had no idea what they really earned. They pivoted to a tool that builds a branded website, qualifies inquiries by voice and handles bookings. Avinash explains his choices: a Ruby on Rails monolith, building slowly, and serving needs rather than wants. Ajith describes what Y Combinator gave them, speed, focus and belief, and why a co-founder relationship rests on trust. They say the hardest part is deciding what to build, since building is now easy. They also keep 10% of the work unautomated, the part that carries the owner's personality. Ajith says what worries him is AI replacing human relationships. Avinash is excited that solo founders can now ship real software.

## Key takeaways

1. Watch what customers need, not only what they ask for. Group repeated requests into patterns and solve ten problems well instead of a hundred poorly.
2. Talk to at least three users every day. Cactus started by looking at a chef's real transactions, which showed she earned half of what she thought.
3. With AI making code cheap, the hard part is deciding what to build, not building it.
4. Choose boring, productive tools such as a Rails monolith, and use AI only where it delivers value, with controls left to the customer.
5. Decide in advance what not to automate. Cactus keeps the owner's personality and relationships as the 10% it leaves alone.
6. A co-founder relationship depends on trust and shared direction first. Division of work comes second, with clear accountability.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> And me and Avnash were meeting with the chef. We asked her, like, how much did you earn last month? And she was like, she gave us a number. And we said, okay, can we just take a look at actually your transactions? And it was half of that, technically. So she was shocked.
> — Ajith, AI with Sach episode 29, at 14:24 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PY8qVlbYHjU&t=864s)

> I think the hardest piece has been actually finding what exactly is it that our customers need. Again, not what, need. So what is it that our customer, what is it that we can provide to our customers that gives them a lot of value? I think that has been more harder than actually building it because these days with AI, you can literally build anything.
> — Avinash, AI with Sach episode 29, at 28:15 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PY8qVlbYHjU&t=1695s)

> You cannot replicate that energy through software. You cannot replicate that energy through a technology, right? And that's the 10% which we don't want to automate. Because that is the soul of your company. And it's usually the founder, right?

# A Bishop’s Take on the Age of Intelligent Machines

Episode 28 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Bishop Thomas Dowd, catholic Bishop of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario (based in Sudbury); former Ericsson telecom employee and early webmaster. A Catholic bishop and former telecom worker on AI, trust, loneliness, free will, the soul and regulation.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 28
- Published: 2025-05-28
- Length: 91 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/28-a-bishops-take-on-the-age-of-intelligent-machines/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY

## Guests

- Bishop Thomas Dowd: Catholic Bishop of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario (based in Sudbury); former Ericsson telecom employee and early webmaster (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/bishop-thomas-dowd/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Bishop Thomas Dowd, who grew up in Montréal, wrote his first program at 12, worked at Ericsson, became webmaster for the Canadian bishops in 1995 and was named a bishop at 40. He now leads a diocese in Northern Ontario. Dowd treats large language models as tools. He has caught ChatGPT filling in blanks, and he describes how an AI trained on Catholic theology gave a parishioner a wrong answer about what the diocese could do. He argues that a machine cannot pray for you. On consciousness, he sets out the Catholic view of the soul, the role of the body in knowing, and free will. He says AI will force us to ask what a soul is. He reads AI boyfriends and girlfriends as a symptom of loneliness that urbanization and social media already worsened, and he warns of a society split by emotional capacity. He wants profit-driven companies regulated, as airplanes and hot dogs are. He ends on honesty and altruism as the virtues we need, and on what a church can offer that cannot be virtualized.

## Key takeaways

1. Treat chatbots as a starting point for research, not a trusted source: check the answer against something you know or a person who knows.
2. An AI is only as good as its training inputs, and copyright limits can keep it stuck on older, worse material.
3. The questions about AI consciousness force a prior question: what do we mean by consciousness, free will or a soul?
4. AI companions meet real loneliness, and companies may profit from it; the risk is people avoiding the hard, risky work of human relationships.
5. Regulation of profit-driven AI makes sense for the same reasons we regulate airplanes, vaccines and meat, and the real danger is people using AI without empathy.
6. Honesty and altruism matter more as technology magnifies their presence or absence.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 29:11 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=1751s)

> a machine cannot pray on your behalf. Like if, if I was going to do a rosary with 150 Hail Marys and I said, well, I don't have time to say 150. I'll just get my computer to say it. No, that's not going to work.

> is everybody going to have an AI boyfriend or girlfriend? No, I don't think so. But if just 1% of the population is experiencing that kind of existential loneliness, well, that's 80 million people. That's a lot of people.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 51:24 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=3084s)

> And so you'll wind up with a stratification of human beings, not based on wealth, not based on intelligence, based on the emotional capacity to enter into relationship with others. What kind of society will emerge from that? I have no idea, but AI could certainly accelerate that big time.

> Not that the AI becomes psychopathic, but that the people behind it are able to use it for just for their own interests with no empathy for anyone else, seeing the human beings interacting with it as ones and zeros, effectively, just as extensions of a system.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 1:09:45 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=4185s)

> I realized I would rather live an uncomfortable truth than a comfortable lie. And it seems so self-evident to me. It was a nice moment, but it seemed self-evident. And I must have been very young, like six or seven or eight.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 1:25:15 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=5115s)

> We had all the money in one week, one week. Because people, what I realized is because people knew who I was and because of the content, it was building a sense of connection. There was also a sense of trust.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 21:56 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=1316s)

> Had I trusted the answer, I would have made errors. And so this is the problem. There's a level of response that can seem true, but which isn't.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 25:10 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=1510s)

> And they said, oh, we can't input that because it's under copyright. So in other words, you can only train your AI on older garbage instead of the newer great stuff. Terrific. What do we need this for?
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 30:19 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=1819s)

> Angels don't have bodies. And so they know what a rose smells like, but they can never actually have the experience of smelling a rose. You know, they could talk about the smell of a rose, but they can't do so from a point of view of experience.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 37:36 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=2256s)

> The profit motive is one that has never really been trusted for pure self-regulation in any circumstance. There's a reason why we have regulatory agencies for the construction of airplanes, right? There's a reason why we have regulatory agencies for the crafting of vaccines or the approval of medications.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 1:06:37 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=3997s)

> I don't think AGI can ever replace the irascible appetite because you want to be the one playing football, not your robot. You know, you want to be the one getting a diploma. If you're in school and you're saying, the reason I want to get a degree is so I can get a good job, why not cheat?
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 1:23:26 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=5006s)

> You can watch it online, but you can't smell the incense online. You know, and there's, you can't receive communion on your tongue online. And we're never sending it by DoorDash.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 1:30:00 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=5400s)

> From my point of view, the critical question is free will itself. None of the atoms of our brain individually possess free will. And so collections of them wouldn't possess it either. That doesn't mean they don't possess randomness.
> — Bishop Thomas Dowd, AI with Sach episode 28, at 44:29 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VvPyFmTgrY&t=2669s)

# Designing the Future of Human Connection — Anick Beaulieu on AI, Creativity & C2 Experiences

Episode 27 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Anick Beaulieu, CEO of C2, the experiential studio behind C2 Montréal. The CEO of C2 explains how her events team uses AI as a creative partner while betting on in-person connection, and why IP limits what clients will buy.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 27
- Published: 2025-05-20
- Length: 30 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/27-designing-the-future-of-human-connection-anick-bea/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoxSNN5rkyY

## Guests

- Anick Beaulieu: CEO of C2, the experiential studio behind C2 Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/anick-beaulieu/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Anick Beaulieu, CEO of C2, an experiential studio that designs B2B events for brands like EY, Amazon and Meta and runs the C2 Montréal flagship. Anick says AI changes events and also doesn't: the goal is still to design meaningful human connections, and AI is a tool to do that better. She is skeptical of the pressure to adopt AI, noting that marketing makes everyone feel behind, and asks what a team is trying to achieve before asking whether to use AI. She sees AI speeding up the path from concept to prototype, but says it will shrink some teams, and that clients hesitate to buy fully AI-made creative work because ownership and IP are unclear. On data, she wants AI to measure emotion at events and trace their long-term effects, such as partnerships that start years later. As a leader, she says AI hasn't changed her style but adds urgency, and that she gives space to staff who know the tools better than she does. She tells a Nike ad story to explain why resisting change doesn't work. The episode ends with a quick-fire round and a plug for C2 Montréal.

## Key takeaways

1. Ask what you are trying to achieve before asking whether to use AI; the goal should drive the tool.
2. AI shortens the path from idea to testable concept, but the human still has to come up with the concept and own it.
3. Unclear IP ownership is a practical limit today: clients hesitate to buy fully AI-made creative work.
4. Leaders who are not tech experts can give space to team members who are, and let their roles grow beyond the original job description.
5. Resisting change outright blocks useful discussion; the productive question is how to adopt AI, not whether.
6. The hardest thing to measure about events is long-term impact, and emotion tracking is one area where AI could help.

# Investing in AI and Impact: Building Resilient Startups in Quebec

Episode 26 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Cédric Beaudoin, senior Associate, impact and technology investing, Investissement Québec (IQ). A Quebec venture investor explains how modular AI, fast iteration and resilience shape the startups he backs, and why everyone should talk about AI.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 26
- Published: 2025-05-05
- Length: 27 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/26-investing-in-ai-and-impact-building-resilient-star/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CLFjfd8UE9M

## Guests

- Cédric Beaudoin: Senior Associate, impact and technology investing, Investissement Québec (IQ) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/cedric-beaudoin/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Cédric Beaudoin, who invests in Series A and later technology companies at Investissement Québec, with a focus on impact. Cédric says he respects entrepreneurs because of the sacrifice and grit the job demands. He describes impact in terms of CO2 reduction, circularity, regional effects and social benefit. For successful startups he points to a long-lasting mission and agility, using Hopper's many pivots as the example. He also argues that shipping something imperfect and fixing it later beats chasing perfection. From his time with the NextAI cohort, he says AI is not new, but the tools and compute are. Startups should build vertical products by assembling existing models into modular software that lets them swap components as better ones appear. He gives two examples: Ready Plan Go for personal tax returns, and Clear Estate for estate planning, where about 40 billion dollars is expected to change hands in ten years. The conversation then turns to how technology can ease an emotionally heavy process while keeping a human in the loop. Cédric names the startup he wishes someone would pitch, a platform linking contractors and suppliers. He closes by arguing that AI is now a feature of every company and that everyone, not only PhDs, should talk about it.

## Key takeaways

1. Impact investors weigh CO2 reduction, circularity, regional effects and social benefit, and CO2 is only the easiest of these to quantify.
2. Resilient startups combine a long-lasting mission with the agility to pivot, as Hopper did many times.
3. Ship something imperfect and fix it later: startups can iterate fast because few people are working on the same large problem.
4. Vertical AI startups can win by building modular software that plugs in existing models and lets them swap one out when a better one appears.
5. In emotionally heavy areas like estate planning, automate the forms and paperwork, and keep a human in the loop to speak the same language as the client.
6. Talk about AI in everyday terms with people around you and start with the tools you can use today, rather than AGI or white papers.

> — Cédric Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 26, at 13:30 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CLFjfd8UE9M&t=810s)

> — Cédric Beaudoin, AI with Sach episode 26, at 16:16 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CLFjfd8UE9M&t=976s)

# L'IA au service de la Cybersécurité avec son Co-fondateur Jean-Sébastien

Episode 25 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Jean-Sébastien, co-fondateur de Fireraven, startup montréalaise de cybersécurité pour l'IA; ancien co-fondateur et CTO de Quotes-n-Go. A Montréal co-founder explains how guardrails and monitoring protect AI chatbots and agents, and warns about lost expert knowledge and data that stays in models. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 25
- Published: 2025-04-09
- Length: 30 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/25-l-ia-au-service-de-la-cybersecurite-avec-son-co-fo/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-U42MCF6dpI

## Guests

- Jean-Sébastien: Co-fondateur de Fireraven, startup montréalaise de cybersécurité pour l'IA; ancien co-fondateur et CTO de Quotes-n-Go (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/jean-sebastien/)

## Résumé

Sach reçoit Jean-Sébastien, co-fondateur de Fireraven, une startup montréalaise qui sécurise et surveille les assistants et agents d'IA. Diplômé de Polytechnique Montréal, il a d'abord cofondé Quotes-n-Go, une plateforme de services d'entretien résidentiel qui estimait les travaux à partir d'images satellites. Il a revendu ses parts pour aller vers la deep tech. Il raconte les débuts de Fireraven en 2023, quand les jailbreaks étaient nouveaux et que presque personne ne pensait à la sécurité des LLM, et comment le cas du chatbot d'Air Canada a montré que le risque était bien réel. Il explique les guardrails sans code : des filtres à l'entrée et à la sortie d'un modèle qui bloquent les sujets hors contexte et font respecter les politiques de l'entreprise. L'erreur la plus fréquente qu'il voit, c'est de ne pas protéger l'entrée du modèle. Selon lui, une startup qui n'a pas encore de clients ne devrait pas investir dans les certifications de cybersécurité. Il compare les accélérateurs Next AI et DTU Skylab, l'un axé sur la croissance rapide, l'autre sur une croissance lente et durable. Il pense que bien des outils B2B de bas de gamme vont disparaître, car l'IA les rend faciles à copier, et que les gens qui ont 20 ans d'expérience dans une niche ont l'avantage. Il termine avec deux mises en garde : le savoir des experts part à la retraite sans être capté, et ce qui entre dans les poids d'un modèle est très difficile à retirer.

## Summary

Sach talks with Jean-Sébastien, co-founder of Fireraven, a Montréal startup that secures and monitors AI assistants and agents. A Polytechnique Montréal graduate, he first co-founded Quotes-n-Go, a home-services marketplace that used satellite images to price jobs. He sold his shares to move into deep tech. He explains how Fireraven started in 2023, when jailbreaks were new and almost nobody was thinking about LLM security, and how the Air Canada chatbot case showed the risk was real. He describes no-code guardrails: filters on a model's input and output that block off-topic requests and enforce company policies. The most common mistake he sees is leaving the input unprotected. He argues that early startups should not spend on cybersecurity certifications before they have customers. He compares the Next AI and DTU Skylab accelerators, one pushing fast growth and the other slow, sustainable growth. He expects many low-end B2B tools to disappear as AI makes copying easy, and he thinks people with 20 years in a niche have the edge. He ends with two warnings: expert knowledge is about to retire without being captured, and anything put in a model's weights is very hard to remove.

## Key takeaways

1. Guardrails work like a firewall on a model's input and output: they block off-topic requests and jailbreaks, and enforce policies such as no financial advice.
2. The most common mistake in company chatbots is an unprotected input; some will reveal their first prompt if you simply ask.
3. The right level of security depends on the use case: a grocery chatbot with no database is low risk, a bank or government chatbot is not.
4. Because AI makes building fast, a product's value now lies in something other than development time, such as network effects, marketing or deep niche knowledge.
5. Data put into a model's weights is hard to remove and can be extracted later, so confidential information needs care before it goes in.
6. Expert knowledge held by people near retirement may be lost unless someone finds a way to capture it, ideally paying them for it.

# The Creator Economy, EdTech, and AI's Impact with Thomas Fortoul

Episode 24 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Thomas Fortoul, host of the Thinking Tech podcast; helping an EdTech startup at Next.ai, Montréal. Thomas Fortoul, host of Thinking Tech, on critical thinking, over-reliance on AI, creators as the new teachers, and education as the lever for the future of work.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 24
- Published: 2025-04-02
- Length: 30 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/24-the-creator-economy-edtech-and-ai-s-impact-with-th/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQaai5qs9io

## Guests

- Thomas Fortoul: Host of the Thinking Tech podcast; helping an EdTech startup at Next.ai, Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/thomas-fortoul/)

## Summary

Sach sits down in person at Next.ai with Thomas Fortoul, a computer science graduate who hosts the Thinking Tech podcast and is working on an EdTech project. Thomas describes his mission as countering information overload in tech and AI. He stays oriented by looking for patterns rather than chasing each new model, by looking at history (the printing press, cars), and by talking with people in executive roles. Both hosts note that the people they interview tend to know themselves well and adapt quickly. Thomas argues that formal education is lagging, that informal learning matters more, and that philosophers and critical thinkers will be the architects of how we work. On the creator economy, he says that as trust in the open internet erodes, people will turn to a few trusted sources, and that content creators are becoming the new teachers. He warns that over-reliance on tools like ChatGPT erodes skills such as writing and reading comprehension. The conversation also covers the idea that AI should involve everyone, an AI and blockchain model where models pay for data, and the areas he is watching: EdTech, legal tech and biotech. He ends with a call to get involved and keep learning.

## Key takeaways

1. Look for patterns and historical parallels (printing press, cars) instead of chasing every new model or buzzword.
2. Knowing what you like and dislike, and following your own goals instead of your peer group's, builds resilience and adaptability.
3. Using AI for everything erodes skills: keep practicing writing and reading, and ask what value you add beyond the prompt.
4. As the internet fills with content, trust concentrates in a few creators, so value creation matters more than reach.
5. Informal and non-formal learning matter more as formal education lags behind.
6. Change starts with conversation and getting involved in your community.

# QuébGPT : Révolutionner les PME avec l’IA – ft Charles Demontigny

Episode 22 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Charles Demontigny, fondateur de QuébGPT (anciennement Fluxion Conseil), créateur du chatbot Capture. A Québec founder explains why SMEs struggle with AI, where Québec stands in the AI race, and what his lead-capture chatbot taught him. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 22
- Published: 2025-02-25
- Length: 26 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/22-quebgpt-revolutionner-les-pme-avec-lia-ft-charles/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk

## Guests

- Charles Demontigny: Fondateur de QuébGPT (anciennement Fluxion Conseil), créateur du chatbot Capture (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/charles-demontigny/)

## Résumé

Sach reçoit Charles Demontigny, fondateur de QuébGPT. Charles a étudié en économie et en économétrie, puis il est tombé dans l’apprentissage automatique et a travaillé comme consultant en analyse de données. Le 1er avril 2023, il lance QuébGPT, un chatbot en blague qui parle québécois et qui devient semi-viral. Il profite de ce bruit pour orienter son entreprise vers les modèles de langage, puis il se concentre sur un seul produit, Capture, un chatbot qui transforme les visiteurs d’un site web en leads qualifiés. Selon lui, les PME n’ont pas vraiment de problème d’IA : elles manquent de clients ou ont des problèmes d’opérations, et un projet sur mesure à des dizaines de milliers de dollars n’offre souvent aucun retour sur investissement. À l’échelle mondiale, il pense que le Québec est en retard sur les modèles de base et pourrait miser sur l’énergie ou sur les applications. Il prévient aussi que des emplois de cols blancs vont disparaître et qu’il faut d’abord aider les gens à se réorienter. Il raconte enfin comment Capture a été paramétré : donner moins d’information au robot a parfois fait mieux convertir. Certains clients obtiennent de 50 à 60 nouveaux leads par mois.

## Summary

Sach talks with Charles Demontigny, founder of QuébGPT. Charles trained in economics and econometrics, drifted into machine learning, and worked as a data consultant. On April 1, 2023 he released QuébGPT, a joke chatbot that spoke Québécois and went semi-viral. He used the attention to move his company toward language models and later narrowed it to one product, Capture, a chatbot that turns website visitors into qualified leads. Charles argues that small businesses rarely have an AI problem. They have too few clients or messy operations, and custom AI projects that cost tens of thousands of dollars often have no return. On the global stage, he thinks Québec is behind on foundation models and could look at energy or applications instead. He also says AI will cost white-collar jobs, so Québec should first help workers transition. He explains how Capture was tuned: giving the bot less information sometimes converted more, because it handed off to a salesperson sooner. He closes with client results, such as 50 to 60 new leads a month for some clients.

## Key takeaways

1. Before building with AI, check that the problem is real: most SMEs need more clients or better operations, not AI for its own sake.
2. A custom AI project costing around $50,000 only makes sense if the return on investment is clear.
3. A chatbot that knows everything about a business can convert worse than one that knows less and hands off to a salesperson.
4. Getting a prompt to work 80% of the time is easy; reaching business goals takes work on UX, knowledge base and connections to other tools.
5. Québec is behind on foundation models and could focus on energy or applications.
6. AI will shake up white-collar jobs, so helping workers change jobs quickly is a priority.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> — Charles Demontigny, AI with Sach episode 22, at 7:58 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk&t=478s)

Ça peut que ça soit abordable ou peu importe, mais il va falloir entraîner les gens à être capables de changer d'emploi rapidement

> il y a quelques années on se vantait au Québec d'être le nec plus ultra de l'IA avec Element AI et juste ça en fait. Il y avait pas mal juste ça. L'Université de Montréal qui avait de la bonne recherche puis force à admettre pas été capable de faire passer cette recherche-là en produit.
> — Charles Demontigny, AI with Sach episode 22, at 10:00 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk&t=600s)

> Peut-être que c'est en dessous parce que, tu sais, on a de la bonne électricité pas chère, peut-être qu'on est capable d'attirer l'entreprise grâce à ça. Puis sinon, c'est peut-être en haut au niveau des applications, de l'applicatif parce que, tu sais, entre le modèle et ce qui va être dans 5-10 ans, les modèles de base, ça va être un peu commodité selon certains.

> la réalité, c'est 95% des visiteurs de site web sont là pour aller chercher de l'information, donc si on a une IA sur notre site pour répondre à ces questions-là, on est capable d'aller répondre à une partie de ces gens-là et de les transformer en clients.
> — Charles Demontigny, AI with Sach episode 22, at 17:30 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk&t=1050s)

> ce qui est bon et pas bon pour nous, c'est faire la job à 80%, c'est hyper simple aujourd'hui. Tu mets un prompt dans un chat puis ça va répondre. Est-ce que ça va atteindre tes objectifs d'affaires la majorité du temps? Non.
> — Charles Demontigny, AI with Sach episode 22, at 19:04 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk&t=1144s)

> — Charles Demontigny, AI with Sach episode 22, at 19:46 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk&t=1186s)

> — Charles Demontigny, AI with Sach episode 22, at 20:40 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-2Z5kTWN3Zk&t=1240s)

> En tout cas, il y a plein de solutions qui finalement ils règlent partiellement les problèmes et ce n'est pas magique.

> je pense qu'on a quand même de la job à faire juste pour nettoyer notre propre chambre à la maison. Peut-être commencer par ça et après ça, si on est capable d'être une société que les gens peuvent regarder et se dire

# The Invisible Labor Behind AI: A Content Moderator’s Fight for Justice

Episode 21 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Kauna Malgwi, former Facebook content moderator (via Sama, Nairobi), leader of the Nigeria chapter of the Content Moderators Union, TIME100 AI 2024 honoree. A former Facebook content moderator describes the hidden human labor and trauma behind AI, and her fight for fair treatment of African tech workers.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 21
- Published: 2025-02-12
- Length: 46 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/21-the-invisible-labor-behind-ai-a-content-moderators/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jAA4BVkzkCs

## Guests

- Kauna Malgwi: Former Facebook content moderator (via Sama, Nairobi), leader of the Nigeria chapter of the Content Moderators Union, TIME100 AI 2024 honoree (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/kauna-malgwi/)

## Summary

Sach speaks with Kauna Malgwi, who fled the Boko Haram insurgency in northern Nigeria and later moderated Facebook content in Kenya for four years through the outsourcing firm Sama. She explains how she was recruited for what was described as a Hausa translation job. She signed a non-disclosure agreement one week into training, before the most graphic material was shown. Moderators earned less than $2 an hour, against more than $20 for similar work in the US and Europe. They had to submit a decision every 50 seconds, even on long videos of beheadings or child abuse, and were penalized for being slow or wrong. Kauna argues Meta knew the psychological cost: the work ran entirely on Facebook's own tools, and counseling was mandatory. She describes foreign workers brought in without work permits and contracts moving from Kenya to Ghana and Nigeria to avoid accountability. She also covers her testimony at the European Parliament on the Platform Work Directive. A psychiatric evaluation of about 140 petitioners found PTSD in nearly all of them. Two years after the layoffs, the court case against Meta is still stuck on jurisdiction. Her core message: AI did not build itself, and the people who trained it need care and recognition.

## Key takeaways

1. AI and social media safety depend on human moderators, often in the Global South, who are rarely acknowledged as part of how AI is built.
2. Deceptive recruitment and early NDAs removed moderators' ability to make an informed choice about traumatic work; transparency is the first fix Kauna asks for.
3. Productivity quotas (one decision every 50 seconds) and pay under $2/hour turn moderation into what Kauna calls forced labor.
4. Outsourcing lets platforms deny responsibility, but the work runs on their own systems, and mandatory counseling shows they know the harm.
5. When legal pressure rises, contracts move to countries with weaker labor laws (Kenya to Ghana to Nigeria), which is why Kauna calls on the African Union to act.
6. Moderator trauma is ongoing, not a single event; care models must address repeated exposure, stigma at home and blacklisting after the job.

# Would you trust it more if it wasn't called AI?

Episode 20 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Mike Todasco, former senior director of innovation at PayPal, inventor with over 100 US utility patents, writer on AI. A former PayPal innovation lead explains why the name 'AI' makes people wary, and why ordinary people and small businesses should just start using it.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 20
- Published: 2025-02-05
- Length: 39 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/20-would-you-trust-it-more-if-it-wasn-t-called-ai/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4Yir9wlsmIg

## Guests

- Mike Todasco: Former senior director of innovation at PayPal, inventor with over 100 US utility patents, writer on AI (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/mike-todasco/)

## Summary

Mike Todasco, who ran the innovation group at PayPal, talks with Sach about a survey he ran on how the label 'AI' changes what people think of a tool. He asked 200 people about driving directions, calling it 'AI' for one half and 'Google Maps' for the other. The AI wording scored 0.5 to 2 points worse on a seven-point scale. Mike traces the name back to the 1950s Dartmouth workshop, where 'artificial intelligence' won because it sounded futuristic and helped with funding. He prefers 'augmented intelligence' and describes today's models as very good autocomplete that works as a tool, not a separate being. He explains why attitudes differ between Japan and the United States, pointing to social media as a source of disappointment in the US. He also names risks: models built to please us, and people getting attached to systems that sound human. His advice is simple. Use the tools, be open about how you use them, and publish a policy on what you will and will not do with AI. He is most excited about small businesses and individuals who can now build software for themselves.

## Key takeaways

1. The word 'AI' alone can lower how favourably people rate a tool: in Mike's survey, the same driving-directions product scored 0.5 to 2 points worse on a seven-point scale when called AI.
2. Treating AI as augmented intelligence, a tool in your workflow, is more accurate and less frightening than treating it as a separate being.
3. Be transparent: label AI-generated images with the model, date and prompt, and publish an internal and external policy on what you will and won't use AI for.
4. Small businesses and startups gain the most: for about $20 a month they get capabilities that once required hiring specialists.
5. Start by using the tools daily, make one the default in your browser and phone, and ask the AI itself how to begin.
6. Keep the downsides in view: models tend to agree with you, and people may bond with systems that sound human.

# AI Transformation: Democratizing Innovation at TELUS

Episode 19 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Alexandre Guilbault, founder of the TELUS AI Accelerator, leading a team of over 65 AI engineers at TELUS. TELUS AI Accelerator founder Alexandre Guilbault explains how to scale AI adoption: solve business problems first, fail fast, hire for soft skills, prepare for agentic AI.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 19
- Published: 2024-12-09
- Length: 31 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/19-ai-transformation-democratizing-innovation-at-telu/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0

## Guests

- Alexandre Guilbault: Founder of the TELUS AI Accelerator, leading a team of over 65 AI engineers at TELUS (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/alexandre-guilbault/)

## Summary

Alexandre Guilbault founded the TELUS AI Accelerator, a team of more than 65 AI engineers working across mobility, home solutions, health and agriculture. He explains that TELUS now wants to put generative AI in the hands of as many employees as possible, because 100,000 people thinking about uses will beat a small expert team. He separates classic machine learning, such as fraud detection, churn prediction and network capacity forecasting, from generative AI co-pilots for IT support, field technicians and call centres.

His main lessons are practical. Stakeholder alignment matters more than the model. Teams should define the business problem before the solution and run proofs of value rather than proofs of concept. Classic ML projects are treated as R&D: test the weakest link first, fail within days, and rank projects by risk-weighted EBITDA. TELUS found that bundling AI with change management created resistance, so each business unit now names a change champion. Squads mix the same roles and are tied to one business unit. Hiring favours curiosity, humility and resourcefulness over credentials. Alexandre advises newcomers to centralize AI talent and to accept that most projects fail. He sees agentic AI, where AI acts as a peer and not only a counselor, as the next wave, with open governance questions. He also argues that management practices must evolve alongside the technology.

## Key takeaways

1. Technology, people and process must change together; the best model is useless if nobody changes how they work.
2. Start from the business problem, not the AI solution, and prefer a proof of value over a proof of concept.
3. Treat classic ML as R&D: test the riskiest assumption first, fail within days, and rank projects by risk-weighted value.
4. Name a change champion inside each business unit so ownership of process change is clear.
5. Hire for curiosity, humility and resourcefulness; in a field that moves this fast, learning speed matters more than credentials.
6. Fund AI as a portfolio, not project by project: if about 80% of data science projects fail, only a portfolio view keeps funding alive.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> I'm often saying the best model in the world is useless if nobody use it or nobody change their process out of that. So sometimes I feel with new technologies coming in, people are so impressed by the technology itself that they forget the principle that has always been there and is still there, that there's no meaningful change without technology, people and process.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 5:45 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=345s)

> POCs are really popular in technology, but a proof of concept finishes with technology concepts. It's not necessarily creating value. So we prefer proof of value. And a proof of value, you might not even have the technology concept completely finalized.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 7:45 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=465s)

> If you don't learn every single day in six months, you're a dinosaur. So even if you hire the best person in the world, but he doesn't have the curiosity, resourcefulness, humility to continue to learn and question others around and read, they will be out of the game within six months and a year.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 20:38 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=1238s)

> But some studies have proven that 80% of the data science project in companies fails to deliver value. So that's four projects out of five that will fail. Finance thinks about funding one project and expects a return on one project. They are more likely not to see the return, and they will stop funding AI.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 25:39 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=1539s)

> We really think that having 100,000 people thinking about the best way to use those technologies is much better than having a small team of experts in the domain trying to figure out how those technologies can really transform business students.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 1:27 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=87s)

> they think a bit like if they have a hammer and they were looking for nails to it. And sometimes it's a little bit too siloed or too narrowed when they think about what could be automated in their task. And automation is something AI can do for sure, but automation will just save you some time. It won't drive a big disruption.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 6:41 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=401s)

> We're trying to ensure that whatever we tackle, if we are to fail, we prefer to fail within a day or two rather than failing after six months. Because there's a huge opportunity cost.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 9:52 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=592s)

> If we have an opportunity of 10 million, but our success rate is of 80%, then it's no longer 10 million. It's 8 million at this opportunity. So something else might become higher and that changes dynamically through time.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 11:17 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=677s)

> And we figured out that there's more resistance to change whenever we come with everything. People like to think of us as an IT support team, a bunch of geeks that are really good with technology, but don't understand the business process.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 14:12 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=852s)

> Actually, we're encouraging them to fail. It's good if they fail. They shouldn't be too hard-headed and try to always be successful or else they're not innovating.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 22:52 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=1372s)

> So I think really AI talent attracts talent. So centralizing will help any business to build this team. Or else if they hire just one or two, they will probably lose those people after six months, a year, and they will start from scratch.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 24:18 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=1458s)

> Agentic AI will be asking a bot to do work. So AI will move from being a counselor to a peer. That will be like everybody will add their peer as an AI, per se. Maybe multiple peers.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 28:10 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=1690s)

> If we structure too much a team, we're killing innovation. So we need to be flexible. We need to reinvent ourselves in management in order to reinvest ourselves in technology.
> — Alexandre Guilbault, AI with Sach episode 19, at 30:49 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YvitzP-4VA0&t=1849s)

# Building Trust Through Responsible AI with Shea Brown (BABL AI)

Episode 18 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Shea Brown, CEO of BABL AI and former astrophysics professor. Shea Brown of BABL AI explains how independent AI audits work, why companies need them, and where to start with risk assessment.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 18
- Published: 2024-12-03
- Length: 38 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/18-building-trust-through-responsible-ai-with-shea-br/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU

## Guests

- Shea Brown: CEO of BABL AI and former astrophysics professor (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/shea-brown/)

## Summary

Shea Brown, CEO of BABL AI and a former astrophysics professor, explains how independent AI audits work and why companies are asking for them. Around 2017, after Cambridge Analytica and biased facial recognition and recidivism tools, he left academia to build a firm that tests and audits AI systems with human flourishing at the center. He describes attestation-style audits, where a company documents what it has done and BABL verifies it through interviews, records, code and test results. He presents risk assessment as the starting point: who the stakeholders are, which features of the system could affect their rights, and which metrics to measure, such as bias or accuracy. He explains why bias testing cannot be cookie-cutter, how explainability helps a human catch problems like zip code acting as a proxy for race, and why systems built on large language models are harder to audit. On regulation, he says compliance usually slows innovation but is still worth it for the trust it earns. He compares the EU, US, Canada, UK, Australia and China. His advice: begin with a basic risk assessment, then align with ISO 42001 and the EU AI Act. Today, enterprise procurement is what pushes most clients to seek an audit.

## Key takeaways

1. Start with a basic risk assessment: list who the system affects, where it could cause harm, and what you will measure, then record it and act on it.
2. Bias testing needs the right metric for the context; an off-the-shelf benchmark rarely fits, so a structured risk assessment should choose the metrics.
3. Explainability helps humans spot failure modes, such as zip code acting as a proxy for race in a loan model.
4. Compliance probably slows innovation somewhat, but innovation that brings value and earns trust is the better goal than innovation alone.
5. Large enterprises increasingly require proof of responsible AI from vendors, so independent audits and certifications like ISO 42001 are becoming a cost of doing business.
6. Larger companies should align with the EU AI Act and ISO 42001; startups should begin with a lightweight risk management system.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> I think compliance will in most circumstances, slow innovation down. So that, that's, that's my take on it. However, I, I still think it's better to focus on compliance because you can innovate quickly, but you can also increase your risk by innovating too quickly.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 24:46 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=1486s)

> the bottom line is if you want to do business with big companies, they have to trust you. And the only really way to do that is to get an independent third party to somehow verify that you are trustworthy
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 33:00 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=1980s)

> Very soon the differentiator is like brand. I trust this brand. And how do you build brand trust? Well, there are lots of different ways, but demonstrating your due diligence and understanding of risks is going to be an important part of that.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 35:34 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=2134s)

> And it could be as simple as just calling a meeting with your friends, your co-founders and saying, Hey, let's sit down in the room for 60 minutes and get a whiteboard out and just try to figure out where could this tool harm people or where could it harm our brand or harm our company and record that and then do something about it.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 37:10 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=2230s)

> a law passed in New York City that required bias audits of automated employment decision tools, but there was no real standard for what that means. So the law had some information about what does it mean to be independent, which is great, although I think a lot of people still were kind of confused about what that means.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 13:26 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=806s)

> And so when we started auditing systems, ChatGPT had not come out yet, or stable diffusion had not come out yet. So generative AI was still something that was just a research exercise that wasn't being used for production systems. And now we're starting to see that many AI systems are built on top of these large language models. And that's a totally different beast to audit.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 15:08 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=908s)

> It's very rare. It depends on the case where it's like, oh, there's this beautiful benchmark. We can just take it and it will tell us what we need to know. Because if that were the case, the client would have probably done it anyway.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 16:32 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=992s)

> And I saw that zip code was a really high, high importance feature. I would automatically tell that that's probably not a great way of categorizing whether somebody should get a loan or not, just because they live in a particular area. And I know it correlates with race, right? At least in the United States.
> — Shea Brown, AI with Sach episode 18, at 21:52 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5CPQWXFepOU&t=1312s)

# AI for Humanity: A Conversation with Allison Cohen

Episode 17 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Allison Cohen, senior applied AI project manager, AI for Humanity team, Mila. Allison Cohen of Mila explains why socially beneficial AI needs slower timelines, community-defined success metrics and wider access to AI education.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 17
- Published: 2024-11-25
- Length: 28 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/17-ai-for-humanity-a-conversation-with-allison-cohen/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg

## Guests

- Allison Cohen: Senior applied AI project manager, AI for Humanity team, Mila (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/allison-cohen/)

## Summary

Allison Cohen, senior applied AI project manager on the AI for Humanity team at Mila, explains what responsible AI looks like when you build tools for real communities. She comes from international development and global affairs, not computer science. She says that background taught her how harmful well-meant interventions can be. Her main argument is that speed works against trust. Moving fast, as Silicon Valley does, leaves little room to work with the people who will use a tool. She also argues that success metrics shape design. In a human trafficking project, usage by police would look good on paper, so the team chose community trust and uptake among survivors instead. She describes Mila's literacy programs, including ones for Indigenous students and for female-plus students, and traces the barriers marginalized groups face from primary school to hiring and promotion. Sach shares a story about AI coaching police officers to de-escalate arrests. Allison answers with concerns about emotion recognition, biased datasets and false positives. She ends with hopes for accessibility and cheaper services, and a call to stay critical of the dominant narrative and to remember the data workers whose exploitation has been ignored.

## Key takeaways

1. Slowing down is often what makes a socially beneficial AI tool work, because trust with the communities who will use it takes time to build.
2. The metric you pick shapes the tool you build: optimizing for clicks or usage can push a project toward the wrong users.
3. Define success with the people who use the tool; in a human trafficking project, that meant community trust rather than police adoption.
4. Ethical risk checks need to be built into the whole AI lifecycle, with time to pause and people with ethics expertise or community representation involved.
5. Barriers to an AI career start early, at the level of school resources and socialization, and continue through university costs, networks, hiring and promotion.
6. Even well-meant AI for good ideas, like emotion detection for police de-escalation, need questions about data diversity, scientific validity and false positives.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> And what I've realized in doing this work is that if we are going to be successful in deploying AI tools that have the type of impact that we're looking to see, we need to kind of move slowly because we need to build trusting relationships with the community groups and individuals who will be adopting this technology
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 7:28 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=448s)

> And how you measure success will end up, of course, having a big impact on how you build these tools. If you're measuring click rate, you may optimize for, um, you know, click bait titles or manipulative tactics. And we don't want to do that.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 10:20 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=620s)

> I also heard how, you know, in certain indigenous schools, there was no science teacher, for example. And so if you're not getting that kind of exposure early on or if you're not socialized to believe you can have a career in this field, there's going to be a number of people that are sort of left behind at that stage.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 17:30 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1050s)

> But because we have decided that the values and priorities of this project are more to serve survivors of human trafficking and support them in rebuilding their lives than it is to support law enforcement agents looking to intervene in a human trafficking case, we've really defined success in terms of community trust and community uptake of the tool.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 20:30 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1230s)

> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 3:45 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=225s)

> there's a lot of interest in moving fast and breaking things, as we know, is the motto that has sort of come out of Silicon Valley. And given how how much of an impact is likely to have and given how scalable that impact really is, there's there's almost this desire to be the first mover to have secured that kind of impact as quickly as possible.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 6:32 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=392s)

> the only way to do that is to make sure you have an organizational structure or set of incentives that allows you to pause and allows you to, for example, work with someone who is specialized in AI ethics
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 11:40 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=700s)

> There is, of course, plenty of controversy around emotional interpretation using artificial intelligence, because what kind of data set are you using and does it predominantly contain instances of white men and women, for example, or men and women from Canada, but then can't generalize to other cultures where emotion might be expressed very differently.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 23:23 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1403s)

> So this is sort of when you start peeling back the layers of whether the tool is going to be human rights respecting in practice, whether it is really AI for humanity or whether it is disguised as being socially oriented, but in reality creates harms that are much more detrimental than the benefits.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 24:29 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1469s)

> maybe, you know, the technology won't replace these professionals fully, but maybe it actually can drive down the cost significantly so that more people can gain access to important services.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 25:37 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1537s)

> But I think it's always important to make sure that we are staying very critical of the narrative that's being put forward. Because, again, we know how exclusionary the field is, and we know how exclusionary it is to sort of be the spokesperson for the field.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 26:54 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1614s)

> I'm thinking about all the examples of the exploitation of data workers and the fact that that's sort of been swept under the rug for a really long time. But I really hope that people start to get more engaged in the field and the barriers to entry start lowering because it's going to continue to have such a dramatic effect on our world.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 27:27 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=1647s)

> I think, to some extent, there's something somewhat Canadian about wanting the technology that we're building to be incredibly human rights respecting.
> — Allison Cohen, AI with Sach episode 17, at 4:31 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8n5nfmghlg&t=271s)

# Transforming Retail Through AI: Inside ALDO's AI Evolution with Fatih Nayebi

Episode 16 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Fatih Nayebi, vice President of Data and AI at Aldo Group and lecturer at McGill University's Desautels Faculty of Management. Aldo Group's VP of Data and AI explains how a traditional retailer builds AI teams, forecasting systems, generative AI tools and data foundations, and measures their return.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 16
- Published: 2024-11-18
- Length: 30 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/16-transforming-retail-through-ai-inside-aldo-s-ai-ev/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo

## Guests

- Fatih Nayebi: Vice President of Data and AI at Aldo Group and lecturer at McGill University's Desautels Faculty of Management (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/fatih-nayebi/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Fatih Nayebi, Vice President of Data and AI at Aldo Group and a lecturer at McGill, about turning a traditional retailer into an AI-powered organization. Fatih describes how his office is organized: data governance, a data platform team, data product teams and a science team, with product managers from each business unit defining the problems. He walks through the revenue growth management program: demand forecasting over a 26-week season, markdown optimization and order fulfillment optimization, built with Evada Labs and partly funded by a Scale AI grant. On generative AI, he covers product and SEO descriptions, an internal RAG assistant for store employees, and a conversational, trend-aware search proof of concept from a hackathon at McGill. The conversation also covers the data problems that slow retail AI, privacy rules such as Law 25 and GDPR, a lakehouse architecture on AWS, how ROI is measured at four levels, and how projects are prioritized. Fatih closes with advice for newcomers: respect data quality, expect experiments to fail, and have people who can explain honestly what AI can and cannot do.

## Key takeaways

1. Sort each problem first: does it need intelligence (a brain problem) or just an application or process fix (a muscle problem)?
2. AI projects stall on data: models need many years of clean, complete, consistent data, not just data good enough for daily decisions.
3. Measure ROI at four levels: bottom-line impact, operational metrics, model metrics, and adoption and usage of the product.
4. Not every experiment reaches production; sometimes the data is missing or expectations are far from results, and teams should plan for that.
5. Agile development alone doesn't cover data practices; data quality, observability and governance have to be built in deliberately.
6. Keep people who can bridge technical and business teams and explain plainly what AI can and cannot do.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> So whatever we have a problem that we want to solve, we look at it from if it's a brain problem, intelligence problem, or is it just a muscle or just application or process problem?

> Many of us, we come from the engineering background with application development experience or data engineering type of background. And sometimes we neglect the importance of the data itself. If we do agile development, agile by itself is not going to take care of the practices around the data. So you need to infuse that.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 27:46 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=1666s)

> We need to experiment things. We need to try things. And not everything that we do is going to go to production because sometimes we find out we don't have the data or the expectations are far from what we're getting.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 28:23 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=1703s)

> So, one of the challenges with Gen.ai today is it's not physically aware. And there are going to be physics-oriented machine learning models that they can understand physicality, dimensions, volumes, the capacities, and so forth to be able to match things accordingly.

But once you want to make machine learning models, you want to have many years of data that are very quality.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 14:19 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=859s)

> One thing for sure is you want to be transparent. You want to showcase how you collect the data, why you collect the data, and what would be for the client in return.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 16:48 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=1008s)

> For machine learning, once you have this established, you don't need ID type of information, right? You want to have a data that is at the aggregate level, can be used for modeling. So, you want the data to be anonymized such that it does not include any identifiable information and then use that for the modeling.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 17:12 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=1032s)

> I see AI to become a UI between the human and the computer, like from the human computer interaction point of view. To simplify many things, we've been doing programming or we've been trying to create all these user interfaces, always to be able to make computers work for us.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 25:05 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=1505s)

> We needed to implement first the fine-tuning, but then later on to implement, you know, with pine cone, a RAG from the scratch. And then finally we moved to the OpenAI's assistance API, and now that's behind the scene.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 8:56 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=536s)

> So, at the end of the day, whatever you do, you want this to have an impact on the bottom line, either through profit or we want to measure the ROI for each of the products that we build. But then, to be able to get there, you always have a sort of operational metric.
> — Fatih Nayebi, AI with Sach episode 16, at 21:02 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlPQdr86RTo&t=1262s)

> The examples I provided to you, like revenue growth management approaches are like, it's just the bread and the butter in the retail. And these are the ones that are the most impactful ones.
