# MonarQ : Le Quantum Québécois - Exploration des Frontières de l'Informatique Quantique

Episode 15 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Suzanne Talon, directrice générale, Calcul Québec. Suzanne Talon of Calcul Québec explains MonarQ, Quebec's first superconducting quantum computer, what it is good for, and why it is still early days. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 15
- Published: 2024-11-04
- Length: 24 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/15-monarq-le-quantum-quebecois-exploration-des-fronti/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0

## Guests

- Suzanne Talon: Directrice générale, Calcul Québec (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/suzanne-talon/)

## Résumé

Suzanne Talon, directrice générale de Calcul Québec, explique ce qu'est un ordinateur quantique et la place de MonarQ, le premier ordinateur quantique supraconducteur fabriqué au Québec, dans l'infrastructure de recherche. Elle compare le bit au qubit et propose une analogie: l'ordinateur classique est une voiture de course, idéale pour aller de Montréal à Québec, alors que l'ordinateur quantique est une montgolfière, idéale pour trouver le centre d'un labyrinthe. Les deux machines vont travailler ensemble, le quantique jouant un peu le rôle de coprocesseur mathématique. Elle décrit le matériel: un cube de 11 pieds de côté qui sert à refroidir, près du zéro absolu, une puce de quelques centimètres. MonarQ compte 24 qubits, bien moins que les machines d'IBM; c'est donc un outil d'apprentissage plus qu'un gain commercial dès demain. Les usages probables touchent l'optimisation (logistique, finance), la chimie et les matériaux, et la cryptographie. Calcul Québec travaille sur le calcul hybride, l'accès pour la recherche, la formation et la vulgarisation. Elle souligne aussi que les chercheurs gardent leur propriété intellectuelle, contrairement à l'accès gratuit aux machines de Google ou d'IBM, et que très peu d'ordinateurs quantiques sont installés dans des centres de calcul dans le monde.

## Summary

Suzanne Talon, executive director of Calcul Québec, explains what a quantum computer is and how MonarQ, the first superconducting quantum computer built in Quebec, fits into the province's research infrastructure. She contrasts bits with qubits and uses an analogy: a classic computer is a race car, good for driving from Montréal to Québec City, while a quantum computer is a hot air balloon, good for finding the center of a maze. The two machines will work together, with the quantum one acting like a math coprocessor. She walks through the hardware: a cube 11 feet on each side that cools a chip a few centimetres wide close to absolute zero. MonarQ has 24 qubits, far fewer than IBM's machines, so it is a tool for learning rather than for commercial gains today. Likely uses are optimization (logistics, finance), chemistry and materials, and cryptography. Calcul Québec works on hybrid computing, research access, training and public outreach. She also stresses that researchers keep their intellectual property, unlike with free access to Google or IBM machines, and that few quantum computers sit in data centres worldwide.

## Key takeaways

1. A quantum computer will complement classical computers, not replace them; think of it as a coprocessor for specific problems.
2. Quantum machines give one answer at the end, so they suit optimization problems where you want only the best answer.
3. MonarQ has 24 qubits and no commercial advantage yet; the goal now is to train people and learn how to integrate it.
4. Hybrid computing is hard: latency, scheduling between classical and quantum, and even incompatible binary formats need international standards.
5. Free access to cloud quantum machines from big vendors can mean the vendor keeps what you run; a nonprofit provider leaves IP with researchers.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> Ce qu'il faut savoir, c'est que l'ordinateur quantique ne va jamais remplacer l'ordinateur classique. C'est vraiment quelque chose qui va être complémentaire. Donc on pourrait le voir en informatique, on va peut-être appeler ça un coprocesseur mathématique.
> — Suzanne Talon, AI with Sach episode 15, at 2:14 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0&t=134s)

Donc, on est vraiment dans l'idée de former, de comprendre, de savoir comment ça fonctionne, pour que dans 5 ans, 10 ans, 20 ans, ce chiffre-là est encore assez inconnu.

Les formats binaires utilisés dans différents champs d'application sont différents. Alors déjà, les binaires de CPU et les binaires des GPU, on parle d'intelligence artificielle, ces formats binaires-là, ce ne sont pas les mêmes.
> — Suzanne Talon, AI with Sach episode 15, at 12:06 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0&t=726s)

> Dans un problème d'optimisation, on a plein de variables, on a un problème complexe, mais le problème classique du voyageur de commerce, quelle est la meilleure façon, ou le problème d'Amazon, quelle est la meilleure façon d'aller livrer 3 millions de colis à 1 million d'adresses, etc., pour être le plus efficace possible.
> — Suzanne Talon, AI with Sach episode 15, at 15:39 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0&t=939s)

Donc, un peu comme tous les outils qu'on utilise, les chats GPT et autres de ce monde ou tout ce qu'on donne à l'ordinateur, bien, voilà, ça part ailleurs.

Il y en a, ça se compte sur les voies d'une main, en fait. En Amérique du Nord, on est les seuls à avoir un ordinateur quantique dans une salle de calcul et de performance.
> — Suzanne Talon, AI with Sach episode 15, at 22:04 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0&t=1324s)

> L'idée, c'est vraiment de venir démocratiser l'outil. Évidemment, encore une fois, c'est quelque chose qui va se faire à long terme, mais l'important, c'est de commencer maintenant parce que c'est des étapes qui prennent du temps, en fait.
> — Suzanne Talon, AI with Sach episode 15, at 22:52 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0&t=1372s)

> mais les coûts de transport sont des fractions énormes des coûts des produits. Donc, si on est capable d'aller améliorer l'efficacité de ce côté-là, on a des impacts à la fois économiques et environnementaux parce qu'on serait capable de réduire les problèmes de transport, par exemple.
> — Suzanne Talon, AI with Sach episode 15, at 19:09 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NqiwsvUX4V0&t=1149s)

# Democratizing Data and AI: Insights from Databricks' Youssef Mrini

Episode 14 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Youssef Mrini, senior Solutions Engineer, Databricks. A Databricks solutions engineer explains data and AI democratization, governance with Unity Catalog, open source compute, and why compound AI systems beat single models.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 14
- Published: 2024-10-07
- Length: 23 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/14-democratizing-data-and-ai-insights-from-databricks/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQcryGgQ1EM

## Guests

- Youssef Mrini: Senior Solutions Engineer, Databricks (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/youssef-mrini/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Youssef Mrini, a senior solutions engineer at Databricks, about what it means to make data and AI usable by people who are not engineers. Youssef explains how Databricks combined its lakehouse (data warehouse plus data lake) with LLM technology from the MosaicML acquisition to form a "data intelligence platform". Non-technical staff can now ask questions in plain English through tools like AI/BI Genie, though he says a human is still needed because models can hallucinate. He names governance as the main blocker to wider access, and describes how Unity Catalog replaced compute-based access controls that were easy to bypass. He also covers Databricks' reliance on open source (Spark, Delta Lake, MLflow), decoupling client from server with Spark Connect, and the work of building RAG applications, which comes down to constant testing. On ethics he is candid that he is not an expert, and points to guardrails and the choice of underlying model. He backs the compound AI systems idea, where several models and tools are combined, and gives concrete uses: document Q&A, support ticket triage, and coding assistants. His closing advice is to pick one topic, learn open source technologies, and practice rather than only read.

## Key takeaways

1. Natural-language querying lets non-technical staff access data, but a human still has to check the output because LLMs can hallucinate.
2. Governance is the main blocker to democratizing data: the right people need access to the right data, and analysts should not be able to change production tables.
3. Access controls tied to compute are easy to bypass; controls tied to the data catalog are simpler to enforce.
4. RAG quality depends on details like chunking strategy, so teams have to keep testing rather than expect a recipe that works.
5. Comparing several models side by side on the same prompt lets you choose per task, which is the practical case for compound AI systems.
6. To keep learning without being overwhelmed, pick one topic, favor open source technologies, and practice instead of only reading.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

# AI and Cybercrime: The New Frontier in Digital Forensics

Episode 13 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Alain Filotto, digital Evidence Specialist, Alphafox Forensics; retired RCMP member and former Chief Operations Officer, TCS Forensics. A retired RCMP digital forensics expert explains how AI changes fraud, policing and evidence, and why everyone should question what they see online.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 13
- Published: 2024-10-04
- Length: 38 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/13-ai-and-cybercrime-the-new-frontier-in-digital-fore/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mq3o0ajQAzs

## Guests

- Alain Filotto: Digital Evidence Specialist, Alphafox Forensics; retired RCMP member and former Chief Operations Officer, TCS Forensics (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/alain-filotto/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Alain Filotto, a retired RCMP officer with 29 years in policing and now a Digital Evidence Specialist at Alphafox Forensics. Alain starts with his career, from pagers and BlackBerrys to child exploitation and national security investigations. His main point is that most cybercrime is old-fashioned fraud that is now faster and reaches more people. AI makes it harder to spot because the broken grammar that used to give scams away is gone. They discuss who is responsible when an employee falls for a phishing email, and why Alain thinks Google should not take ad money from scammers. They cover how police use AI, from identifying victims to analysing cameras, and the ethical limits of surveillance, using the Paris Olympics as an example. Alain argues that private forensic firms will take on more work, and that international cooperation remains slow. He warns that using AI to detect fakes also teaches it to make better ones. On open source versus closed AI, he thinks you cannot put the genie back in the bottle. His advice is practical: do not click links you did not expect, and verify everything before you react.

## Key takeaways

1. Most cybercrime is traditional fraud made faster and cheaper, so the basic rules still apply: if you did not expect a payment request or a link, do not act on it.
2. AI removes the old tells of scams, like bad grammar, so people need verification habits instead of relying on spotting mistakes.
3. Companies share responsibility for fraud: they should filter threats, train staff, and test them with fake phishing emails.
4. Using AI to detect fakes also feeds the models that make fakes, so detection tools are never a final answer.
5. Policing is a cat-and-mouse game, and slow cross-border cooperation and lab backlogs push work toward the private sector.
6. The most useful skill against AI-enabled fraud is the habit of questioning and double-checking before reacting.

# L'IA et le droit : Enjeux éthiques, risques et régulation

Episode 12 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Céline Castets-Renard, professeure titulaire à l'Université d'Ottawa et titulaire de la Chaire de recherche sur l'IA responsable dans un contexte mondial and Jade Benson-Poitras, étudiante en droit, stagiaire chez Rexlex et assistante de recherche à l'Université d'Ottawa. Two law researchers explain how Canada, the EU, the US and China regulate AI, and why existing law already applies. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 12
- Published: 2024-09-24
- Length: 40 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/12-l-ia-et-le-droit-enjeux-ethiques-risques-et-regula/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FcwK41CZ8aU

## Guests

- Céline Castets-Renard: Professeure titulaire à l'Université d'Ottawa et titulaire de la Chaire de recherche sur l'IA responsable dans un contexte mondial (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/celine-castets-renard/)
- Jade Benson-Poitras: Étudiante en droit, stagiaire chez Rexlex et assistante de recherche à l'Université d'Ottawa (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/jade-benson-poitras/)

## Résumé

Sach reçoit Céline Castets-Renard, titulaire de la Chaire de recherche sur l'IA responsable, et Jade Benson-Poitras, étudiante en droit et assistante de recherche. On commence par le mandat de la chaire : faire du droit comparé entre le Canada, les États-Unis et l'Europe pour nourrir la réflexion des législateurs. Céline distingue les risques à court terme (discrimination, exclusion dans les outils d'immigration, révision humaine) des risques existentiels évoqués par Yoshua Bengio. Selon elle, le juriste doit d'abord s'occuper des risques actuels. Jade insiste sur l'urgence de légiférer au Canada, où le projet de loi C-27 avance lentement en comité, et au Québec, où les travaux du Conseil de l'innovation n'ont mené qu'à dix principes non contraignants. Céline décrit trois modèles de régulation : étatique en Chine, centré sur le marché aux États-Unis, centré sur les droits en Europe. Les invitées abordent aussi la loi 25, les risques pour les élections, le rôle d'OpenAI dans l'établissement des normes et l'épisode des images de Gemini. Sur la question de réglementer ce qu'on ne comprend pas complètement, Céline propose de cesser d'ouvrir la boîte noire et d'imposer des obligations avant et après la mise en marché, avec une surveillance continue. Elle rejette la personnalité juridique de l'IA, qui déresponsabiliserait les humains. Jade conclut en invitant les étudiants à apprivoiser l'IA.

## Summary

Sach talks with Céline Castets-Renard, who holds the Research Chair on Responsible AI, and Jade Benson-Poitras, a law student and research assistant. They start with what the chair does: comparative law between Canada, the US and Europe, with the aim of informing legislators. Céline separates short-term risks (discrimination, exclusion in immigration tools, human review) from the longer-term existential risks raised by Yoshua Bengio. She says jurists should first deal with the current ones. Jade stresses the urgency in Canada, where Bill C-27 has been slow in committee, and in Québec, where the innovation council's work has produced only ten non-binding principles. Céline describes three regulatory models: state-led in China, market-led in the US, rights-focused in Europe. They discuss Québec's Law 25, risks to elections, OpenAI's role in setting norms, and Google Gemini's historically absurd images. On regulating what nobody fully understands, Céline says to stop trying to open the black box and instead set obligations before and after market release, with continuous monitoring. She rejects legal personhood for AI because it lets humans avoid responsibility. Jade ends with advice for students: learn to work with AI.

## Key takeaways

1. Existing law (privacy, consumer, intellectual property, anti-discrimination) already applies to AI. A new technology does not suspend it.
2. Regulating a black box means setting obligations on the data before release and on the results afterwards, with monitoring across the whole life cycle.
3. Regulatory models follow history and culture: China puts the state first, the US the market, Europe individual rights, and Canada is pulled between the last two.
4. Giving AI legal personhood would let developers dodge responsibility, so providers should be held to obligations of means: test, monitor, alert users, withdraw faulty tools.
5. Large general-purpose models are concentrated in a few firms because only they have the data, infrastructure and money, which raises competition concerns.
6. Law students and professionals should learn to use AI rather than fear being replaced by it.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

Par contre, ce qu'on peut faire et ce que l'on doit faire, c'est poser des obligations avant et des obligations après la boîte.

# Littératie numérique à l'ère de l'IA : Défis et opportunités pour les employés - Benoit Aubert

Episode 11 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Benoit Aubert, professeur à HEC Montréal, chercheur au CIRANO (ancien directeur de la Roe School of Business et de l'École de gestion de l'information à l'Université Victoria de Wellington). Benoit Aubert explains why basic digital literacy matters more than AI expertise for most jobs, and why automating entry-level tasks threatens how workers build expertise. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 11
- Published: 2024-09-16
- Length: 25 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/11-litteratie-numerique-a-l-ere-de-l-ia-defis-et-oppo/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QMPuAGqawXw

## Guests

- Benoit Aubert: Professeur à HEC Montréal, chercheur au CIRANO (ancien directeur de la Roe School of Business et de l'École de gestion de l'information à l'Université Victoria de Wellington) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/benoit-aubert/)

## Résumé

Benoit Aubert, professeur à HEC Montréal et chercheur au CIRANO, définit la littératie numérique comme la compréhension de base des outils numériques et des données, et il rappelle que les employeurs ne peuvent plus la tenir pour acquise. Son équipe a analysé des offres d'emploi au Canada : on y demande surtout des outils bureautiques, des bases de données, Excel et les médias sociaux. Les postes en apprentissage machine existent, mais ils sont peu nombreux. Selon lui, les entreprises ont souvent une bonne vision de leur transformation, mais elles échouent à l'atterrissage : on envoie une formation en ligne aux employés et on suppose qu'ils sont prêts. Sur l'IA, il ne cherche pas à rassurer. Des emplois vont disparaître, et l'automatisation des tâches d'entrée retire la voie qui permettait de développer son expertise et d'accéder à la gestion. Personne n'a encore trouvé le chemin de remplacement, admet-il. Il compare le moment à la révolution industrielle, mais cette fois, ce sont les mêmes personnes qui vivent l'avant et l'après. Il relie aussi le sujet au faible investissement et à la productivité des entreprises canadiennes, et il met en garde contre les barrières tarifaires qui gardent en vie des entreprises peu productives. Ses conseils : utiliser l'IA, garder un humain dans la boucle, explorer, comparer avec ce qui se fait à l'étranger et ne pas être complaisant.

## Summary

Benoit Aubert, professor at HEC Montréal and researcher at CIRANO, defines digital literacy as a basic understanding of digital tools and data, and argues employers can no longer take it for granted. His team analysed Canadian job postings and found that employers mostly ask for office tools, databases, Excel and social media. Machine learning roles exist but are few. He says companies often have a clear vision for a transformation but fail at the landing: employees on the ground are given online training and assumed to be ready. On AI, he does not offer reassurance. Some jobs will disappear, and automating entry-level tasks removes the way people used to build expertise and reach management. He admits nobody has yet found the replacement path. He compares the moment to the industrial revolution, but notes that this time the same people live through the before and the after. He also links the issue to low Canadian investment and productivity, and warns against tariffs that keep weak firms alive. His advice: use AI, keep a human in the loop, explore, benchmark abroad, and avoid complacency.

## Key takeaways

1. Digital literacy (office tools, databases, Excel) is what Canadian employers actually ask for, far more than machine learning skills.
2. A transformation fails at the landing: sending online training to employees does not mean they can use the new tools.
3. Automating entry-level tasks with AI removes the path people used to take to build expertise, and companies risk having no managers in ten years.
4. Use AI yourself to learn its limits, and keep a human in the loop for responsibility and quality of decisions.
5. A digital transformation is a rethink of how a company works and what it offers, so training has to be part of the investment.
6. Employers should explore, test ideas at industry forums and benchmark against what is done abroad.

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> — Benoit Aubert, AI with Sach episode 11, at 8:15 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QMPuAGqawXw&t=495s)

# Will AI Make Universities Complacent? - Nabil Beitinjaneh

Episode 10 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Nabil Beitinjaneh, faculty Lecturer and Academic Program Coordinator, McGill University School of Continuing Studies. A McGill educator explains how AI changes learning, which skills matter, and why job displacement and weak regulation need collective answers.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 10
- Published: 2024-09-09
- Length: 65 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/10-will-ai-make-universities-complacent-nabil-beitinj/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s-gC9irOk9o

## Guests

- Nabil Beitinjaneh: Faculty Lecturer and Academic Program Coordinator, McGill University School of Continuing Studies (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/nabil-beitinjaneh/)

## Summary

Nabil Beitinjaneh, who coordinates programs at McGill's School of Continuing Studies, talks with Sach about AI and education. He sees real gains: personalized tutoring, better course preparation, and predictive analytics that flag students at risk. He also names the costs. Students can feel they understand more than they do. Personalized tools can create filter bubbles. Learning, which is often hard and uncomfortable, may get skipped. He says nobody yet has a vision for the future of education, so universities must experiment, as his own courses do by letting students use generative AI to code.

The talk then turns to work. He expects AI to augment individuals but replace some jobs at the macro level, especially intermediate roles. He uses outsourcing, Uber and the Luddites to show how displacement hurts people and how hard it is to fund answers like UBI. He argues that ethics without regulation has no teeth, and that citizens rarely read the bills they are invited to comment on. He lists the risks as privacy, bias, concentration of power, opacity, and loss of human agency. For individuals he recommends AI literacy plus domain expertise. For organizations he recommends governance, clear accountability, and diverse teams.

## Key takeaways

1. AI can give you answers that create an illusion of learning, so educators need new ways to check what students actually know.
2. Learning that is hard and sometimes painful is part of how people learn, and personalized AI tutoring can remove it.
3. Pair AI literacy with domain expertise: without knowing a field, you do not know what to ask the AI.
4. Ethics discussions matter but have little force without regulation, and citizens rarely use the chance to comment on draft laws.
5. Job displacement will not be solved by one actor; it needs government, companies, schools and workers thinking together.
6. Organizations should set clear accountability for AI errors and give people a career path, not just add the technology.

# Transforming Ecommerce with Generative AI: Insights from Natalija Pavic from Salesforce

Episode 9 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Natalija Pavic, product marketing leader and Alliances strategy lead for Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Salesforce; host of the Salesforce Commerce Cloud Innovations podcast. A Salesforce product marketer explains where generative AI is useful in ecommerce today, where it falls short, and why trust and data policy matter.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 9
- Published: 2024-09-03
- Length: 35 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/09-transforming-ecommerce-with-generative-ai-insights/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i81L27IJxyQ

## Guests

- Natalija Pavic: Product marketing leader and Alliances strategy lead for Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Salesforce; host of the Salesforce Commerce Cloud Innovations podcast (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/natalija-pavic/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Natalija Pavic, who leads alliances strategy for Salesforce Commerce Cloud and holds a patent on generative promotions. She says generative AI is at the "bulletin board" stage of the internet: the technology exists, but the big use cases have not been defined yet. In ecommerce, the current uses are merchant productivity tools, such as generated product descriptions, promotions written from plain-language requests, and copilots, plus chat assistants and natural-language search for shoppers. She explains how her patent grew out of automotive incentives that pulled sales forward without making money. Other topics include optimizing products so GPT recommends them, as businesses once did for SEO, and prompt engineering as a new skill. She also covers the human in the loop and citations as ways to reduce hallucinations. She is critical of image generators that lack diversity and warns that "democratization" of data can hide a loss of privacy. On jobs, she uses the chess example to argue that people who learn to work with AI benefit most. Her advice to companies is to start small, test internally, and tell customers clearly where AI and their data are used. She also says AI behaves like brute force, so data volume and quality matter more than the algorithm.

## Key takeaways

1. Generative AI is early: like the first years of the internet, the major use cases are not defined yet, so experimenting now is useful.
2. Product data quality matters. Clean, complete product attributes and outside mentions help GPT-style assistants recommend your products, as SEO did for Google.
3. Human review and citations are practical ways to keep generated product descriptions on brand and accurate.
4. Be careful with calls to democratize data. Set a privacy policy on who can access what, and tell customers where AI and their data are used.
5. Start with small, low-risk tests such as a landing page or a pop-up. Using the tools also gives you a say, because vendors build what customers pay for.
6. Do not tune the algorithm endlessly. Feed the model more of the right data and put gates in place so it does not find fake correlations.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

But actually, overall, they may have been losing money.

> When Deep Blue came out, there was like a whole scare of like, oh no, now it's like chess is not, you know, chess is going to be replaced by robots. But like nobody wants to watch robots play chess with each other. So that wasn't the thing.

> prompt engineering is now the new skill. Right before it was like, oh, coding. Now it's like, actually, how do I create the prompt that's going to give me the result that I'm interested in? It's actually a new skill that we now have to learn in addition to it helping us.

> — Natalija Pavic, AI with Sach episode 9, at 31:42 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i81L27IJxyQ&t=1902s)

> — Natalija Pavic, AI with Sach episode 9, at 33:29 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i81L27IJxyQ&t=2009s)

# Vers une IA Responsable avec Olivier Blais, VP Science Décision chez MoovAI

Episode 8 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Olivier Blais, cofondateur et VP Science décisionnelle chez MoovAI; président de la délégation canadienne pour l'IA à l'ISO/IEC et auteur de la norme ISO 25058. Olivier Blais of MoovAI explains how to manage AI responsibly: bias, transparency, accountability, ISO standards, and why limiting automation can be the safer choice. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 8
- Published: 2024-08-27
- Length: 44 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/08-vers-une-ia-responsable-avec-olivier-blais-vp-scie/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WIukbcUoUxM

## Guests

- Olivier Blais: Cofondateur et VP Science décisionnelle chez MoovAI; président de la délégation canadienne pour l'IA à l'ISO/IEC et auteur de la norme ISO 25058 (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/olivier-blais/)

## Résumé

Olivier Blais, cofondateur et VP Science décisionnelle chez MoovAI et président de la délégation canadienne pour l'IA à l'ISO/IEC, explique ce que l'IA responsable veut dire concrètement. Il préfère parler de gestion responsable de l'IA, parce que c'est une technologie dont les utilisateurs ne connaissent pas toujours les données d'entraînement ni le fonctionnement. Il montre comment les biais s'installent : des outils d'embauche qui favorisaient les hommes blancs d'un certain âge, le code postal utilisé comme indicateur dans le crédit, la détection faciale des premiers iPhone qui avait du mal avec les peaux plus foncées. Il rappelle qu'un biais n'est pas toujours négatif : c'est ce qui permet de distinguer les camions qui ont besoin d'entretien des autres. Ses solutions : se poser les questions de risque dès le départ, puis tester les cas extrêmes. À partir de projets réalisés avec la STM et Metro, il explique l'importance de la qualité, de l'adaptabilité et de la transparence, et pourquoi on n'est jamais obligé d'automatiser 100 % d'une décision. Côté responsabilité, plus on automatise, plus l'organisation qui a bâti le système en répond. Il parle aussi du rôle du Canada dans la norme ISO 42001, de la tension avec les règles européennes et du défi de l'IA générative, qui n'a plus de portée définie. Il est optimiste : une industrie d'outils de conformité s'en vient, et chaque personne est responsable de son propre usage de l'IA.

## Summary

Olivier Blais, cofounder and VP of decision science at MoovAI and chair of the Canadian delegation for AI at ISO/IEC, explains what responsible AI means in practice. He prefers the French phrase "responsible management of AI", since AI is a technology whose training data and inner workings users often don't know. He describes how bias creeps in, using hiring tools that favoured older white men, postal codes used as a proxy in lending, and early iPhone face unlock that struggled with darker skin. He explains that bias is not always negative: it is what lets a model discriminate between trucks that need maintenance and trucks that don't. His fixes are risk questions at the start, then testing edge cases. Using real projects with the STM and Metro, he shows why quality, adaptability and transparency matter, and why you are never obliged to automate 100% of a decision. On accountability, he argues that the more you automate, the more the organisation that built the system is liable. He also covers Canada's role in ISO 42001, the tension with European rules, and the new difficulty that generative AI has no defined scope. He is optimistic that an industry of compliance tools is coming, and says every person is responsible for their own use of AI.

## Key takeaways

1. Responsible AI is better understood as responsible management of AI: know the data, the purpose, and who governs the system after launch.
2. Bias isn't always harmful: it is how a model tells cases apart. It becomes a problem when it rests on unjustified assumptions, such as using a postal code to judge someone's ability to repay a loan.
3. Reduce bias by asking risk questions at the start, then testing extremes (a 100-year-old applicant, an 18-year-old asking for a huge loan) and restricting predictions where data is thin.
4. You are never required to automate 100% of a decision. The more you automate, the more liability shifts to the organisation that built the system.
5. Transparency concerns the model, and interpretability concerns a single prediction. Users need enough of both to trust the tool, and you must check how people actually use it after launch.
6. Generative AI breaks the old compliance habit of defining a narrow scope, so new ways of assessing risk are needed.

# l’Avenir de l’IA au Québec avec Anne Nguyen, Directrice IA au Conseil de l’innovation du Québec

Episode 7 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Anne Nguyen, directrice IA au Conseil de l'innovation du Québec. Anne Nguyen explains how the Conseil de l'innovation du Québec pushes practical, responsible AI adoption across Québec's businesses and regions. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 7
- Published: 2024-08-21
- Length: 18 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/07-lavenir-de-lia-au-quebec-avec-anne-nguyen-directri/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_LJkMl8Bx_k

## Guests

- Anne Nguyen: Directrice IA au Conseil de l'innovation du Québec (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/anne-nguyen/)

## Résumé

Sach reçoit Anne Nguyen, directrice de l'IA au Conseil de l'innovation du Québec, pour faire le point sur l'IA dans la province. Elle décrit son rôle comme celui de fédérer l'écosystème, des chercheurs comme Yoshua Bengio jusqu'aux grandes entreprises. Après la réflexion collective de l'an dernier sur l'encadrement d'une IA responsable, le Conseil se concentre cette année sur l'adoption : formation, littératie en IA et retour aux cas d'usage concrets. Anne veut que l'IA ne soit plus vue comme une affaire montréalaise. Elle rêve de campagnes régionales, comme Gaspésie prêt pour l'IA, avec des applications pour la pêche au homard, la cueillette des bleuets ou les mines. Pour les entrepreneurs, le plus grand obstacle est le manque de temps. Elle définit l'IA comme un outil appliqué à un problème, et présente la transparence et l'explicabilité comme le cœur d'une IA responsable. Aux jeunes, elle dit qu'il n'est pas nécessaire de savoir coder et que les historiens et les philosophes ont leur place. Elle suit avec intérêt l'apprentissage continu et l'IA quantique. Face à la peur de perdre son emploi, elle compare la situation à la révolution industrielle et rappelle qu'un humain doit juger si un résultat a du sens. Elle conclut par un appel à la diversité et à l'inclusion.

## Summary

Sach talks with Anne Nguyen, AI director at the Conseil de l'innovation du Québec, about where AI stands in the province. She describes her job as bringing the AI ecosystem together, from researchers like Yoshua Bengio to large companies. After last year's collective work on a framework for responsible AI, the council now focuses on adoption: training, AI literacy and a practical push toward real use cases. Anne wants AI to be seen as more than a Montréal story. She imagines regional campaigns such as Gaspésie ready for AI, with applications for lobster fishing, blueberry picking and mining. She names lack of time as the main obstacle for entrepreneurs, defines AI as a tool applied to a problem, and explains transparency and explainability as the core of responsible AI. She tells newcomers they do not need to code and that historians and philosophers have a place. She is excited about continual learning and quantum AI. On job fears, she compares the moment to the industrial revolution and insists that humans must decide whether results make sense. She ends with a call for diversity and inclusion.

## Key takeaways

1. Treat AI as a tool applied to a specific problem, not as a solution in itself.
2. You do not need to know how to code to work in AI; multidisciplinary teams need historians, philosophers and social scientists.
3. For many small businesses, the main barrier to adopting AI is time, so AI literacy and simple entry points matter.
4. Responsible AI rests on transparency (knowing the data and algorithm behind a result) and explainability, which has to be balanced against intellectual property.
5. AI adoption can be built region by region, around local industries like fishing, blueberries or mining.
6. Fear of AI can create a digital divide, so including people from diverse backgrounds is a condition for lasting adoption.

Puis ça, c'est un défi parce que tu peux dire, « Ah, la transparence à tout prix, oui, mais il y a quand même de la propriété intellectuelle.

# Democratizing AI Education: A Conversation with Timothy from the AI Launch Lab

Episode 6 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Timothy, co-Founder and Managing Director of the AI Launch Lab; member of the AI Advisory Board at Dawson College. Timothy of the AI Launch Lab on training college students in AI through real projects, who gets shut out of the field, and why AI's current harms matter more than AGI.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 6
- Published: 2024-08-14
- Length: 62 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/06-democratizing-ai-education-a-conversation-with-tim/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BLdihbA-D2g

## Guests

- Timothy: Co-Founder and Managing Director of the AI Launch Lab; member of the AI Advisory Board at Dawson College (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/timothy/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Timothy, co-founder of the AI Launch Lab, a Canadian non-profit that trains people for AI work through hands-on projects and internships. Timothy explains how it grew out of a Concordia student association in 2018, survived the pandemic funding cuts through Quebec government grants, and now focuses on college students with partners Dawson College and Mitacs. He describes why project-based learning keeps pace with AI tools that change monthly, why 75% of their cohorts come from underrepresented groups, and how companies still tend to hire only PhDs or young people. They then discuss responsible AI as a business advantage, and Timothy's reluctance to spend time on AGI speculation compared with present harms. He raises the Apple Card credit disputes, opaque lending algorithms, and the entry-level jobs disappearing first. Using the Luddites as an example, he argues that people are now artisans who learn to use the machines, and that ordinary social and political pressure will be needed to avoid a dystopia. He ends by urging people outside AI, especially those with domain knowledge, to get involved.

## Key takeaways

1. Project-based training keeps up with AI better than textbooks, because the tools and models change monthly or even weekly.
2. LLMs have cut routine data cleaning in student hackathons from about a day and a half to a few hours, so college students can now deliver real value to companies.
3. Many companies still hire only PhDs for AI work, yet many AI projects do not need that profile; diversity of background changes what gets built.
4. Ethical and responsible AI can be a business advantage: it lowers litigation risk and prepares companies for coming regulation.
5. Opaque algorithms in lending and hiring, like the Apple Card disputes, show why current harms deserve more attention than AGI speculation.
6. Entry-level jobs are the first to be stripped away, so building skills early and bringing domain expertise into AI matters.

# How to Revolutionize Data Engineering with Diana, the AI-Powered Jr Data Engineer

Episode 5 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Josh Gray, co-founder and CEO of Artemis. Artemis CEO Josh Gray explains Diana, an AI junior data engineer, and argues that AI agents will add to data teams rather than replace them.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 5
- Published: 2024-08-06
- Length: 19 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/05-how-to-revolutionize-data-engineering-with-diana-t/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sbf72Bo3vAQ

## Guests

- Josh Gray: Co-founder and CEO of Artemis (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/josh-gray/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Josh Gray, co-founder and CEO of Artemis, a Vancouver startup that builds Diana, an AI agent working as a junior data engineer. Josh defines an AI agent as a smart helper that uses the software you already have and does the work, instead of waiting for you to fill in forms. He walks through a broken-pipeline example: Diana reads the error logs, finds the cause, writes the fix and opens a pull request in GitHub, showing every step along the way. On jobs, he relies on a argument from Box founder Aaron Levie: companies are capital constrained, so a team that gets more done earns more and ends up hiring more, not firing. He says AI agents make mistakes because the software is non-deterministic, so users need an interface that exposes every step and makes errors quick to fix. He describes knowledge graphs as a map that tells Diana where to look in a company's data models. Other topics include a healthcare client, a claim of 15 hours saved for 5 to 10 delegated tasks a week, a planned public benchmark for data engineering agents, and his advice to dive into AI now, since he sees real value being built behind the hype.

## Key takeaways

1. An AI agent is software that uses your existing tools and does the task, rather than a tool you have to fill in by hand.
2. Transparency matters most when AI changes code or does calculations: users need to see sources, steps and even the agent's own mistakes.
3. Agents are non-deterministic and will err, so the interface must make errors easy to spot and fix.
4. The case against layoffs: if a team gets more done with the same people, revenue grows and the team can grow too, though some small teams may still shrink.
5. Giving an AI context about your data models and warehouse, for example through a knowledge graph, is what lets it act like a veteran engineer.
6. Data engineering has few public evaluations for agents, unlike software engineering, which makes benchmarks a gap worth watching.

# How to Reclaim Your Time with Jamie, the AI-Powered Meeting Assistant

Episode 4 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Benedikt, co-founder of Jamie, an AI meeting assistant (previously co-founder of TeamTap). Jamie co-founder Benedikt explains how an AI meeting assistant works, how it handles European data rules, and how to validate a startup idea.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 4
- Published: 2024-07-31
- Length: 15 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/04-how-to-reclaim-your-time-with-jamie-the-ai-powered/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpVgRi5xtf8

## Guests

- Benedikt: Co-founder of Jamie, an AI meeting assistant (previously co-founder of TeamTap) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/benedikt/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Benedikt, co-founder of Jamie, a Berlin-based AI meeting assistant. Benedikt tells how he and his co-founder Luis met playing tennis, started a first product called TeamTap, and then built Jamie to solve a problem they felt themselves: taking meeting notes while trying to listen. Jamie listens to a call or an in-person meeting without a bot joining, then produces action items, decisions, a customizable summary and a transcript. A sidebar lets users ask questions across their past meetings. Benedikt explains that they launched an imperfect first version in 2022, personally onboarded a couple of hundred customers, and grew through SEO and close contact with users. On regulation, he says Jamie is GDPR compliant, stores no audio permanently, does not train on user data and hosts data in Germany. He sees AI as a productivity driver if companies invest in education, because many people are still afraid of it. His advice to founders: do not treat polite interest as validation. Launch a simple MVP, or get contracts signed before you build.

## Key takeaways

1. Solving a problem you have yourself brings more passion than solving one for strangers.
2. Launching an imperfect first version early gives the feedback needed to build a solid core product.
3. Personally onboarding early users and staying in touch with them is a growth channel as well as a learning one.
4. Polite interest is not validation: ship a simple MVP, or get people to sign contracts or pay before you build.
5. For an AI tool used at work, privacy choices (GDPR, no training on user data, EU hosting) can be a selling point.
6. Companies adopting AI need education and clear guidelines, because the first reaction of many employees is fear.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

# How Salesforce is Using AI to Transform Customer Relationships

Episode 3 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Jag, senior Solutions Engineer, Enterprise, Salesforce (data and AI specialist). A Salesforce solutions engineer explains how AI is added to CRM, why trust and humans in the loop matter, and why he expects a return to human connection.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 3
- Published: 2024-07-24
- Length: 23 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/03-how-salesforce-is-using-ai-to-transform-customer-r/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA

## Guests

- Jag: Senior Solutions Engineer, Enterprise, Salesforce (data and AI specialist) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/jag/)

## Summary

Sach talks with Jag, a senior solutions engineer at Salesforce, about how AI is being built into customer relationship management. Jag starts with his background in data analytics and his view that the more useful question is what remains once the AI hype settles. He compares it to Napster, which made music abundant and less valued, followed by a rise in vinyl sales. He describes Salesforce tools such as Prompt Builder, Copilot and a vector database. He gives an example from a mining company that cut its response time for bid documents (RFIs) from 175 days to under 30 using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). He explains the trust layer between the language model and customer data, the audit trail, and why a human stays in the loop for B2B uses. He sees RAG as an underdog technology and the AI boom as a comeback for plain machine learning. He expects healthcare and law to be disrupted. He says he would like an AI spam filter so real emails stand out, and admits he sometimes jumps to ChatGPT before listening to a customer's question. He ends by asking listeners to think about what they want automated in two years, and to accept being imperfect.

## Key takeaways

1. Ask what remains of an AI use case once the hype fades, not only what is exciting now.
2. Salesforce puts a trust layer between the language model and customer data: no training on customer data, an audit trail of queries and toxicity detection.
3. RAG over past documents can cut very long, repetitive work, such as a bid response going from 175 days to under 30.
4. In serious B2B settings, AI replaces tasks, not people, and a human stays in the loop.
5. Much of the current AI boom is classic machine learning (regression, likelihood to close) under a new name.
6. Before reaching for ChatGPT, listen to the question first; being empathetic is a skill AI can erode.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> if we go back to circa 2000 when Napster came out, right? And everybody was like, this is the next big thing. We're just not going to pay for music anymore, right? And what happened out of that? We had unlimited, abundant access to music. But it also made us less excited and less happy. Every time we heard a new song, we valued each song less.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 4:08 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=248s)

> So we were able to unlock access to all that wealth of information in those previous RFIs using RAG because we're feeding that data back into the vector database so that when a new RFI comes in, it automatically looks at the questions in this new RFI and finds the closest match to the answers from previous RFIs. So something that used to take 175 days to fill out now takes less than 30.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 11:55 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=715s)

> the biggest winner out of this whole AI boom, has been technology that's decades old, which is like machine learning. So customers that weren't taking machine learning seriously a few years ago are using AI as a scapegoat to do something that's been around for a long time.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 18:37 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=1117s)

> I would love to see like an AI email spam filter so that we go back to just drafting real emails. And this is kind of odd as me saying as a Salesforce solution engineer, but I think it will help the people that desire human connection stand out versus the ones that may have taken a shortcut.

> I think we're jumping to solutions before listening. And I find myself doing this when a customer is asking me a question. I got ChatGPT open and I'm already trying to understand the answer to it rather than trying to understand the question in much more depth than I used to.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 20:48 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=1248s)

> think about which parts of your life you want automated in AI in two years, not just what you want automated tomorrow. And think about the psychological impact every time you want to use AI versus just intuition or using human interaction. And desire to be perfectly imperfect rather than be perfect.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 22:26 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=1346s)

> Why? Because at the end of the day, anything that gets too popular too quick hits diminishing returns. And we go back to something that's more natural to us.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 4:38 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=278s)

> we built out our own trust layer, as we call it, and essentially a firewall between any LLM and Salesforce. And it has a couple of main tasks. One is to make sure that the LLM does not get trained on customer data. So that retention stays on the Salesforce side boundary.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 13:33 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=813s)

> Because we're dealing with B2B customers. It's not like a Spotify recommendation. This is really serious shit, right? Like, am I recommending a promotion to a customer that probably isn't entitled to one? Could that be bleeding dollars out of the business?
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 14:42 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=882s)

> there was a few articles about is AI, does AI mean the death of structured relational databases? I don't think so. I think we desire structure and we desire the visibility to the structure.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 17:05 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=1025s)

> I think in the healthcare and life sciences industry is going to be disrupted hardcore for good reason. Like a radiologist may be able to use AI to detect cancer much, much earlier than they used to before. They'll still be a human in the loop, but they'll be able to get some assistance from AI.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 19:27 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=1167s)

> quantifying human behavior can mean like, if you are a musician, how do you read the crowd? That's quantifying human behavior, which is using your natural senses rather than using an algorithm. So essentially, my goal was to kind of learn how to build an API into someone's mind.
> — Jag, AI with Sach episode 3, at 3:09 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8-UnJLq6NYA&t=189s)

> he's saying that AI shouldn't replace a job, but rather a task from a job to make it easier for the worker.

# How Fuse is Transmuting the Energy Crisis into Opportunity

Episode 2 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features JC Btaiche, CEO and founder of Fuse, a fusion energy company based in Canada. JC Btaiche explains how Fuse uses pulsed power to pursue fusion energy, and why AI's growing appetite for electricity makes that work urgent.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 2
- Published: 2024-07-24
- Length: 15 minutes
- Language: English
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/02-how-fuse-is-transmuting-the-energy-crisis-into-opp/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls

## Guests

- JC Btaiche: CEO and founder of Fuse, a fusion energy company based in Canada (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/jc-btaiche/)

## Summary

Sach talks with JC Btaiche, CEO and founder of Fuse, a Canadian fusion company. JC explains fusion in plain terms: reproducing the conditions inside the sun for a few nanoseconds. Fuse does this with what he calls a lightning bolt in a bottle, a pulse of stored energy released very fast to implode fuel. He traces his path from a childhood wish to build a fusion-powered rocket, helped by a father trained as a nuclear physicist, to a conviction that energy underpins human prosperity. He links GDP per capita to kilowatt hours available per capita. JC describes Fuse's milestones: the first licence in Canada for its type of fusion generator, a new pulse power machine tested over 100 shots, and early commercial revenue, which sets it apart from firms betting on energy in 7 to 10 years. He presents Titan, a pulse power driver that could make fusion facilities a third of the size, five times cheaper and twice as energy efficient. He frames the future through Vaclav Smil's energy ages, argues for tracking the rate of progress instead of a date, and notes the defence roots of the technology. He closes by inviting listeners to a live firing of Titan on August 8.

## Key takeaways

1. Fusion copies how the sun works: compress light atoms under extreme pressure, density and time until they fuse and release energy.
2. AI and quantum computing are pushing energy demand up sharply, which is why new energy sources matter to the AI story.
3. GDP per capita tracks the kilowatt hours available per capita, so energy access shapes prosperity, especially in emerging economies.
4. Fuse's approach, pulse power derived from decades of national lab research, aims to make fusion facilities smaller, cheaper and more efficient.
5. Some fusion companies bet on commercial energy in 7 to 10 years. Fuse sells technology and earns revenue today while maturing the science.
6. JC suggests judging fusion by its rate of progress and iteration rather than by a promised date.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> So it's like creating an artificial sun on Earth and putting it in a bottle. And you can imagine that's pretty challenging. And so for us, the way we create those conditions that are, you know, star-like or sun-like conditions, you know, we create essentially a lightning bolt. So essentially creating a lightning in a bottle that, you know, implodes a kind of fuel.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 2:59 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=179s)

> I think it's the last energy source that humanity will ever need. And especially as the technologies like AI, quantum or others are starting to wrap up, the world's demand for energy is growing exponentially. And so we believe fusion is going to be the answer for the energy needs for our civilization.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 1:05 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=65s)

> So I went to the Internet and started Googling, like, how to do interstellar travel in a timely manner. And, you know, there are some folks, really cool people who have spent a lot of time thinking about this and came up with this fusion-powered rockets. And so that's when I said, I want to build a fusion-powered rocket.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 4:07 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=247s)

> Even if you think basic things like GDP per capita, it's directly tied to kilowatt hour available per capita. So how do we kind of get the whole world to prosper? I think fusion and energy is at the core of, like, human prosperity.

> taking a bet that in 7 to 10 years there's going to be commercial energy. And that's all that, you know, we're working very hard to get there as fast as possible, but we're making revenue today. And so we're building a sustainable business and maturing the technology to get to fusion energy eventually.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 6:22 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=382s)

> And why Titan really matters is it can make any next generation fusion facility based on the Titan technology at least one third the size or at least five times cheaper and doubles the energy efficiency. It was much more scalable as an approach.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 7:18 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=438s)

> Like there's the age of the like muscles, right? When we were using cows or our own, you know, muscles and humans to do work. And then we went into the chemistry time, right? Where the chemical energy era, we're trying to do, you know, combustion and railroad, just combustion and different, you know, different ways to generate heat and then through heat produce energy.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 8:41 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=521s)

> Because even if you think about, you know, fossil fuels, a lot of people talk about how bad they are for the environment, et cetera, which they definitely have lots of cons. But, you know, fossil fuels are also very useful to producing plastics, to producing different materials and molecules that are really, really useful for humanity and basic necessities.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 9:29 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=569s)

> Like if you wake up and you have more energy, right, then you don't have to worry about turning off the light or how much your compute power is. Like energy becomes a commodity that I think will have significant impact on like human flourishing, innovation, et cetera.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 13:23 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=803s)

> I think like what really matters here rather than like putting a date is actually measuring the rate of progress. But I think it took decades to get to some big milestones. But I've seen right now, especially with the surge of there's six billion dollar, over six billion dollar at this point announced publicly at least.
> — JC Btaiche, AI with Sach episode 2, at 11:15 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBjTBsnkls&t=675s)

> So there's really awesome technology that was built through national security and defense programs that, you know, it's time to commercialize. # La Révolution de l'IA avec MoovAI

Episode 1 of AI with Sach, a podcast hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal, features Guillaume Petitclerc, co-fondateur et VP Marketing et Partenariats, MoovAI (aussi CMO et co-fondateur de Snitch AI). A MoovAI co-founder explains why AI projects fail on adoption rather than technology, and why the first project, governance and human contact matter. The conversation is in French.

- Show: AI with Sach, hosted by Sacha Gucciardo in Montréal (https://aiwithsach.com/)
- Episode: 1
- Published: 2024-07-10
- Length: 25 minutes
- Language: French
- Page: https://aiwithsach.com/episodes/01-la-revolution-de-l-ia-avec-moovai/
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc

## Guests

- Guillaume Petitclerc: Co-fondateur et VP Marketing et Partenariats, MoovAI (aussi CMO et co-fondateur de Snitch AI) (https://aiwithsach.com/guests/guillaume-petitclerc/)

## Résumé

Sach reçoit Guillaume Petitclerc, co-fondateur de MoovAI, une firme montréalaise qui déploie des modèles d'IA existants pour des entreprises clientes. Guillaume raconte l'origine de l'entreprise en 2018 : Montréal avait une recherche de pointe, mais très peu se rendait jusqu'aux entreprises. MoovAI voulait démocratiser l'IA au Québec et au Canada. Il présente des projets pour Métro (prédiction des produits frais dans plus de 100 épiceries), Pratt & Whitney (maintenance prédictive et liste de clients à appeler) et le Collège Sainte-Anne (un outil de correction de textes qui libère du temps pour que les professeurs expliquent les fautes). Son idée centrale : les échecs en IA sont rarement technologiques. Ils viennent d'un mauvais change management, d'utilisateurs qui n'ont pas été impliqués et d'un premier projet raté, qui peut retarder l'innovation de plusieurs mois, voire de plusieurs années. Il parle aussi de gouvernance et de politiques d'utilisation de l'IA générative, d'IA responsable chez MoovAI (formation du Mila, norme ISO rédigée par son associé) et du recrutement de jeunes talents. Sur la société, il reste optimiste si la réglementation et la formation suivent, mais il s'attend à ce que les cols blancs soient touchés en premier. Selon lui, le contact humain, surtout à l'école, est irremplaçable. Son conseil final : ne faites pas ça tout seul.

## Summary

Sach talks with Guillaume Petitclerc, co-founder of the Montréal firm MoovAI, which deploys existing AI models for business clients. Guillaume explains the 2018 origin of the company: Montréal had strong research, but little of it reached businesses. MoovAI set out to make AI accessible to Québec and Canadian companies. He describes projects for Métro (fresh-product prediction in over 100 grocery stores), Pratt & Whitney (predictive maintenance leads) and Collège Sainte-Anne (a text-correction tool that frees teachers to explain mistakes). His main argument is that AI failures are rarely technical. They come from poor change management, from users who were not involved, and from a bad first project that sets innovation back by months or years. He also covers the need for governance and usage policies for generative AI, responsible AI at MoovAI (Mila training, an ISO standard written by his partner), and hiring young talent. On society, he is optimistic if regulation and training are in place, but expects white-collar workers to be hit first. He believes human connection, especially in schools, cannot be replaced. His closing advice to companies is not to do it alone.

## Key takeaways

1. AI projects rarely fail because of the technology. They fail on adoption and change management, so involve end users from the start.
2. The first AI project matters most: a failure gives skeptics an argument and can delay innovation for months or years.
3. Treat AI as a tool tied to a business goal, not something to buy for its own sake.
4. Generative AI is like shadow IT: companies need governance and usage policies before employees paste any information into any tool.
5. Responsible AI is decided project by project, starting with whether a project should be done at all.
6. Get help from people who have already delivered AI, internally or through a partner, because the technology moves too fast to follow alongside daily operations.

## Verified quotes

Each quote is checked word for word against the recording.

> L'IA, c'est un outil. Donc, tu ne vas pas aller t'acheter un marteau pour aller t'acheter un marteau. Tu vas t'acheter un marteau parce que tu as besoin de planter des clous. Donc, il y a plusieurs objectifs d'affaires qui ne sont pas répondus par l'intelligence artificielle aujourd'hui.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 10:43 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=643s)

> C'est rarement un problème technologique. Parce que, bon, on est la race humaine et les gens en technologie habitués, c'est-à-dire les outils sont là. À mon sens, puis ce qu'on a vu sur le marché, c'est surtout l'adoption et beaucoup du change management.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 11:44 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=704s)

> Tu sais, si tu donnes un nouvel outil à des vendeurs qui est basé sur l'intelligence artificielle, puis ces gens-là font ça depuis 20 ans, puis ils n'ont pas été impliqués dans le projet dès le départ, ils vont faire, il est beau ton outil, mais je ne vais pas l'utiliser. Pas de retour sur investissement.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 12:10 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=730s)

> On le sait, cette révolution-là de l'intelligence artificielle va toucher les cols blancs beaucoup plus que les cols bleus, qui est une des premières révolutions de cette ampleur-là et de cette rapidité-là dans le marché du travail.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 19:17 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=1157s)

> Et donc, « Don't get me wrong », la recherche fondamentale est super importante, mais on ne voyait pas le lien, le pont de cette belle recherche-là où le gouvernement du Québec et du Canada ont investi des millions de dollars pour développer des nouvelles technologies. Et lorsqu'on se retournait dans notre monde, dans le monde du travail, bien, il n'y avait rien.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 2:04 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=124s)

> Un bel exemple qu'on avait fait avant l'IA générative, on avait même utilisé GPT-2 pour le faire. Donc, le modèle qui est un peu l'ancêtre de GPT-4 qui tourne derrière ChatGPT. Et donc, l'idée, c'était de reproduire l'intelligence ou la façon de parler de Noam Chomsky, le philosophe américain.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 4:17 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=257s)

> Je pense qu'on voit de moins en moins de mégaprojets de 20 quelques millions de dollars pour faire un simple modèle ou une simple solution d'intelligence artificielle. Je pense qu'on va plus se diriger vers des portfolios de plein de produits.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 4:56 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=296s)

> Donc, pour aider les professeurs à corriger les textes de leurs étudiants, ce qui va permettre aux professeurs de passer plus de temps avec l'étudiant à lui expliquer ses fautes, plutôt que de passer du temps à corriger les divers textes qui sont rédigés par leurs étudiants.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 6:44 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=404s)

> On a fait un projet il y a de ça quelques mois avec Métro, donc la chaîne épicerie. C'est un système de prédiction des produits frais, donc tout ce qui est viande, fruits et légumes. Et c'est utilisé en ce moment au-dessus de 100 épiceries au travers du réseau.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 7:36 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=456s)

> L'année 2010, on parlait de shadow IT, donc de faire un petit channel slack sur le côté alors que ton organisation va utiliser officiellement Microsoft Teams. Mais l'idée est un peu la même avec l'IA dans le sens où l'organisation doit se doter d'une gouvernance, doit se doter de règles, de politiques d'utilisation de l'IA générative.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 9:07 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=547s)

> Parce que le pire qui peut arriver dans les organisations, on le remarque, il y a souvent un ou une championne, donc quelqu'un qui promeut l'intelligence artificielle à l'intérieur de l'organisation. Puis si le premier projet se plante, bien là, tu as tous les gens autour qui vont dire, c'est en 2022 puis ça n'a pas fonctionné, etc.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 9:51 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=591s)

> Mais il reste quand même que, dans le cas de l'école, surtout, le contact humain, la relation avec le professeur, la façon du prof de comprendre puis de réexpliquer l'information pour solidifier les apprentissages chez les jeunes. C'est sûr que c'est, à mon sens, irremplaçable.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 22:00 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=1320s)

> Faites pas ça tout seul dans votre entreprise. La technologie avance à un rythme beaucoup trop effréné pour être en mesure de suivre ça et des opérations quotidiennes. Donc, ce serait ça mon dernier conseil.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 24:28 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=1468s)

> On a formé tout notre staff avec une formation du Mila sur justement, ça s'appelle Trel, sur l'IA responsable. Et comment on fait? On a la chance aussi d'avoir Olivier Blais, mon associé, le CTO de Mauvais-Eye, qui a littéralement écrit la prochaine norme ISO sur l'intelligence artificielle.
> — Guillaume Petitclerc, AI with Sach episode 1, at 13:56 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcQrfTdkjRc&t=836s)
